ARC: The Chunchu Era (643–654)

=== EPISODE 40: Gi (起) (645)
Chunchu decides to travel to the East, guided by his friend Takamuko no Kuromaro.
Munhee packs for him. She has packed for every trip he’s ever taken. She will pack for one more. Nobody writes any of this down, which is why it needs saying.
munhee: How many months this time?
chunchu: …I don’t know.
munhee: Then I will pack for more.
The King of the East receives him politely, which is its own kind of answer.
kotoku: Baekje — the Land of the Heavenly Deer, Land of the Lord Buddha — is our ally. / With respect — I must refuse peace with the Divine Country.
chunchu: Baekje is a country on its way to ruin…
chunchu: Our sacred country has produced no end of talent, / and yet not one man the equal of Goryeo’s Gesomun.
kotoku: You… speak our language remarkably well.
chunchu: Sun Tzu says the highest strategy is to win without fighting. / If Chunchu may add one word: if fight you must, the highest strategy is to fight by borrowing another’s hand. / Too many of Silla’s young men have already died…! / How am I to face their parents?
He asks for troops. He asks twice.
kuromaro: Chunchu… do you truly mean to go begging to every country around you? / Even Yamato has heard of the Eternal General and the Sword of the Divine Country. Silla may not be the power it once was, but we have strength enough to fight Baekje and Goryeo ourselves.
haesang: If you reach the eastern islands, my lord, ask after their lacquer. / And if you reach Chang’an again — ask after a woman who finishes the emperor’s sentences. Merchants hear weather early.
## The Harmony Council
An old High Councillor still holds the first chair. Under him sit six councillors, Yushin and Bidam among them. They still decide only by unanimity. It’s the only way this council selects anything.
The technique has not changed since they crowned Dukman: initial vote, deliberation, final vote. Six Councillors. One High Councillor. Nothing moves unless the circle closes.
[diagram harmony-council]
Then the room turns to the question everyone has been circling: when Her Majesty fails, who next. The Sacred Bone has thinned to a sister. Someone says the name Princess Seungman the way you set a cup down that you expect everyone to drink from.
One by one the hands go up. In a unanimous council a raised hand is a kind of weather — once it starts, it finishes. Yushin’s hand is among them. He has served one queen; he will serve her sister.
Only one hand stays down.
Five pieces go to the yes side of the cup. Bidam’s piece stays on the no side.
[diagram harmony-council]
murim: Bidam. This is the initial vote. / Five are up. What is there to deliberate. / We cannot even open the final vote. / You locked the door.
suljong: One hand down and this room is finished. / You know that, and you still put it down?
bidam: I object.
The room does the small silence of men who have already counted themselves finished. Unanimity has failed. The name cannot pass. Someone laughs once, short, the laugh you make when a junior spoils a dinner.
alchun: Bidam… alone? / It is Princess Seungman.
bidam: Princess Seungman is not as clear-sighted as Her Majesty. / We cannot hand the country over for Sacred Bone alone. / Thirteen years ago, when I stood for Princess Dukman, it was because she was the cleverest. / Now you ask me to throw that measure away.
yushin: Bidam. / Same blood. Same house. / The sister of the queen you raised.
bidam: That is why I object all the harder. / Brother. / We are one hundred and eight to one hundred and eight from our Hwarang days. / A country is not a scoreboard. / On a night when Lord Chunchu’s eyes turn toward Chang’an — if we seat another soft Sacred Bone, who sells this country.
Yushin does not answer the count. Something in his face closes that has been open since they were boys on the yard. The Council adjourns with no successor named.
[FLASHBACK 610 The higher teaching · 아비달마]
  Class 51’s first morning. Packed earth still dark. Bidam is sixteen. His father walks him as far as the yard gate and no further — Musan hall does not hover.
  sukwon: Bidam… / Do you know the meaning of your name.
  bidam: Yes, father… / I was named after the Abhidharma, the higher teaching. It—
  sukwon: Yes… the higher teaching. / And as a young man, and as a Hwarang, your duty is to uphold that. / And remember this: / Even if no one else agrees with the truth… even if speaking it out loud causes others to defame and mock you… / You must always walk toward the truth, in isolation if you must. There is no other way. / You may have heard the saying: upon victory, a king; upon defeat, a traitor. / 성즉군왕 패즉역적. / Son… I need you to be a man who would rather be a righteous traitor than an unrighteous king. / Bidam… I love you…! / Go make us proud, son…!
  He does not name the Gaya-born boy who will share the class. He only ties Bidam’s headband once, tight, and lets the gate take him.
In the emptied hall the incense has burned down to a stub. Bidam has not left the table. His fist is still on the wood.
## Princess Seungman
Princess Seungman catches him at the palace gate. Word has reached her before he has.
jinduk: Bidam…! What is this I hear? / Surely not…
bidam: Our sacred country has produced no end of talent, / and yet not one man the equal of Goryeo’s Gesomun.
He starts counting who would come with him, and the first door he knocks on is Alchun’s.
bidam: The problem is these rotten ministers!
alchun: Oi. Enough of that ignorant talk. / The level of the ministers is the level of the country. / If the people were clear-sighted, the ministers would notice and do their jobs.
bidam: What are you talking about! / Do you look down on the people of this sacred country? / They have always—
alchun: Yes. I look down on them. So what? / If everything is this rotten and you lie there doing nothing, some of the blame is yours. / Why is it always the most ignorant in a country who shout loudest that it is the greatest…
alchun: …And use your head. If Princess Seungman doesn’t take the throne, who sits there? Chunchu. He’ll take it himself.
bidam: I have already heard that Lord Chunchu says he will not.
alchun: Chunchu is the most cunning man in Samhan…! / Never — not for one moment — believe a word that comes out of that mouth…!
Before the month is out, Supum is thanked for his years and sent home, and the queen makes High Councillor of the one man who told her council no.
That night Bidam takes the old black headband out of the chest where he keeps it. There is still blood on it, gone brown with the years. He does not remember whose.
bidam: …I gave this to that boy, back then. / Told him nobody would trouble him if he had it.
bidam: I did not know the one troubling him would turn out to be the country.
## Yumjong
Bidam does not recruit with speeches, whatever the Council thinks of him. He recruits with tea and long silences, and the first man to drink the tea is Yumjong, a True Bone whom nobody has ever accused of anything, because nobody has ever noticed him.
yumjong: How many men, Councillor?
bidam: A paddy is not planted in a morning, Yumjong. One shoot, and then the next, and then the water does the rest. / Enough for the Fortress of Radiance. By the time Her Majesty’s breath runs out.
yumjong: And the Marshal?
bidam: Yushin stands where the Queen stands. He always has. / When she is gone he will stand where the next one stands, and he will call it loyalty, and he will even be right.
yumjong: He’s not even Silla, you know. / Gaya. His great-grandfather handed over Geumgwan with the keys still warm. The men in the outer works would like hearing that.
Bidam’s beads stop. He has said the word to Yushin’s face a hundred times on the yard, and Yushin has laughed every time. He has never heard it said like this, by a man who means it as a door.
bidam: …Careful, Yumjong. / A word you shout at a man’s gate comes back to your own. Gaya.
He says it once more, under his breath, as if testing the weight.
Gaya. A word six hundred years old that still cuts a marshal. Where did it come from? Six eggs, falling out of the sky…!

=== EPISODE 41: Suro (42) [flashback]
This is the story of the Gaya confederacy.
Gaya doesn’t have a crown. It has a league of iron harbours, six of them, give or take. No one king can lock the vote. Surabol would find that exhausting.
[diagram gaya-league]
Before the sons, there is a look from very high up. Ibiga keeps the sky the way other gods keep a hall — cloud is his body, the living world a map he does not usually read. Then he looks down.
On her mountain the Lady of the Right View is on watch. At first she is the ridge — jade stone, mist, a woman’s shape the mountain has not admitted yet. The mountain is a woman before it has a face. Then a face comes out of the stone. She is guarding the mountain as if it were a country. She does not look up. She does not need to. Then the sky occupies the path. Cloud comes down to the ridge.
ibiga: That ridge… / That woman. / I have flown this path a thousand times. Why is the mountain looking back.
Love arrives as weather — sudden, unasked. He cannot keep the hour. He falls before he lands. The sky comes down to touch the mountain, and does not leave.
ibiga: Mountain. / Your shoulder… is warmer than cloud. / Your waist… steeper than cliff.
jeonggyeon: Why has heaven come down. / To look? / Or… to touch. / If to touch… kneel first.
ibiga: To touch. / I looked… and could not hold back. / The knees… already are.
jeonggyeon: Then closer. / Ridges do not keep guests long. / Tonight I will make an exception. / I will keep your mouth… at my throat.
ibiga: Your name… Right View. / The longer I look, the less rightful my thoughts become. / I want to put heaven… between your thighs.
jeonggyeon: Then stay wrongful. / Nights when heaven kneels on a mountain… are not so common. / Kneel. / All the way.
Cloud covers the ridge. What happens under it is not for the song. By the time the cloud thins, neither of them is kneeling, and neither of them has let go.
He holds her with one arm. The other is cloud. The ridge is still a mountain; the mountain is still a woman. She does not look up. She does not have to.
By morning the ridge remembers two gods who would not let go. From that heat come eggs, and from the eggs, kings.
The sky god Ibiga and mountain goddess Lady of the Right View give birth to two sons, King Suro and King Ijinasi.
On Earth, the people sing a song to call for a new king.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 2, Wonder 2 — King Suro / Turtle Song; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 158] Turtle, turtle — show your head. If you do not, we will roast and eat you.
The people find a box of six eggs. Six babies hatch, Suro and Ijinasi among them. They found six kingdoms:
herald: …Eggs, you said?
herald: Six. In a box. From the sky.
Nobody in Samhan finds this remarkable. Silla’s founder came out of an egg. Goguryeo’s founder came out of an egg. Here are six more. At some point one has to ask what the birds were doing.
Queen Heo, an Indian princess, becomes the first queen of Golden Gaya.
She arrives on a red-sailed ship at twenty-one — foreign, luminous, built like nowhere on this coast. The beach is only a door. The first time Suro falls in love is not on the sand.
In the timber court of Golden Gaya she presents herself — no servant speaking for her, her own name, silk that does not belong to this hall. He is already on the dais. He meant to receive a princess. He receives a woman, and love hits him before protocol can stand up.
Protocol is still trying to stand. He is already off the dais. He comes down with one arm — gold around violet, the same hold the sky used on the ridge, only this time the hall has columns and a floor.
Servants had been sent to the ship. She refused them. So the court is where they meet — and the moment he sees her, speech leaves him like heat from an open kiln.
heohwangok: Have you come to fetch me… / or have you already begun to take me. / With your eyes. / Your mouth… looks dry.
suro: … / ……You. / Your mouth…
heohwangok: Yes. / My mouth. / When the king looks at me like that… I get warmer. / Your hands… where do you mean to put them. / Even if you can’t speak — your hands know.
suro: Your waist… / I mustn’t… / If I touch…
heohwangok: Then touch. / Since the king can’t choose… I’ll choose for you. / Here. / And here. / You’re shaking.
suro: …Hungry… / I can’t… speak…
heohwangok: Then don’t speak. / If you’re hungry… take me first. / Slowly. / Not like a king — like a man.
He makes a sound that is nowhere near a word, and she smiles as if it were the only answer she came across the sea for.
On the hill she offers her silk trousers to the mountain spirit. He watches as if the rite were meant for him alone — jaw tight, hands useless at his sides.
suro: …How will we know the mountain accepted it?
heohwangok: I can tell from the king’s eyes. / You look like someone who has already received.
suro: …It is not I who received. / …I am going mad wanting to.
heohwangok: This country. / And by tonight… its king.
Two nights in a tent by the water before anyone may say marriage. By the second dusk he can barely keep his voice steady when she says his name — and she says it into his mouth so he has to swallow it.
She turns so he can see the curve of her hip catching lamp, and he is kissing the throat he will marry before he has permission to call it a country.
When he turns to the lamp she looks at the width of his back — muscle under purple-gold silk, a king’s body that the court never sees — and does not hide how that look sits on her mouth.
heohwangok: Slowly. / Your tongue — here. / The way you say my name. / The lower lip. / Below that. / More.
suro: …At this rate I will learn the language. / Or I won’t. / I think I will fall apart first. / Inside you…
heohwangok: Then fall. / That way I have to put you back together every night. / With hands. / With mouth. / Until the king is a king again.
The lamp burns low. She has taught him a dozen words since the dais, and in the dark she teaches him the rest without any — her hand on his wrist, showing him where, laughing when he is slow, then not laughing at all. She is twenty-one and crossed a sea with a stone pagoda in her ship’s hold to stop the waves; he is a king who hatched from an egg and has never once been told how. Neither of them is a god tonight. They are clumsy and greedy, and by the second hour they are good at it.
suro: Say it— say it again— / In your Ayuta tongue— my name— / …I have forgotten what my own country is called—
heohwangok: My king— more— / Haa— my country has no word for this either— / Not yet— don’t go—
The second night she is on top, violet silk off her shoulders and the gold tiger-pins still in her hair, because she refuses to take them out for a man who cannot yet say good morning in her language. He loses his own words again. She keeps hers. When she comes apart she says something in the tongue of Ayuta that nobody on this coast will ever translate, and he decides it was his name.
heohwangok: My king’s— ah— / Stay— just like that—
suro: …Wife. It is morning. / I cannot… take my hands away.
heohwangok: I know. / But I have not yet learned this country’s hours.
suro: …The ministers are outside. / Before I go in… once more.
heohwangok: Once? / What a modest king.
suro: I am not modest. / …I am only holding on. / Barely.
heohwangok: It does now. / I brought it with me — that sound, that night.
They are married a hundred and fifty years — the record is firm about this and entirely untroubled by it — and have ten sons. She asks that two of them carry her name instead of his. He agrees without an argument, which in the whole of this history is the single strangest thing any king does.
heohwangok: My country is gone. Only the name is left.
suro: Then we keep the name. I can always make another country.
She dies at a hundred and fifty-seven. He follows ten years later and asks to be laid where he can see her hill.
Ten days of grain. One dying queen. One banner on the Radiance wall. Start counting…!

=== EPISODE 42: Seung (承) (647)
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Seondeok, yr. 16 (647), 1st month; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 122] Bidam, Yeomjong and others said a woman sovereign cannot govern well, and so plotted rebellion and raised troops, but did not succeed.
## DAY 1
Queen Sunduk (52) is in critical condition. The Eastern Palace smells of medicine and of a succession nobody has settled.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Queen Seondeok knows three things in advance; Ha & Mintz tr., p. 73 · Ilyeon, Lee Byong-do ed., p. 98] I shall die in such a year, on such a month and day. Bury me in the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.
Princess Seungman sits on the edge of the sickbed with a comb, because somebody has to do the Queen’s hair and the maids’ hands shake. They are cousins, five years apart, the last two Sacred Bone women in the world, and they have been doing each other’s hair since the younger one was tall enough to reach.
jinduk: Hold still, unni. / …You’ve gone thin at the temple. When did that happen.
sunduk: While you weren’t looking. That’s when everything happens. / Pin it high. If I’m going to the Thirty-Three Heavens I want to look taller than the gods.
jinduk: Don’t. / Don’t talk about where you’re going like it’s the market.
sunduk: …Seungman-ah. You’ll have to sit in it. / I’m sorry. It’s a hard chair. I’ll leave you a cushion.
Seungman pins the binyeo high, exactly where the Queen asked, and does not answer, which is the only way she has ever won an argument with her.
Bidam and Yumjong raise men at the Fortress of Radiance. The slogan is old. They only give it a banner. Yumjong holds the outer muster. Bidam walks the rampart as if the stones owed him rent. Inside the palace, the stewards count the grain and arrive at ten days. Nobody says the number aloud. Everybody schedules by it. The rebels tie on black headbands, Bidam’s old colour from the yard, so they can tell their own from the palace blue.
He carries the heavenly-horse sword in the dark. The robe eats the lamp. Only the ring pommel holds the light — a gold circle at the end of old-hall steel.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin (Bidam’s rebellion, 647); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2] Bidam and the others encamped at Myeonghwal Fortress; the royal army camped at Wolseong. Attack and defence lasted ten days without being broken.
Before the banner goes up he lights a stick of incense on the rampart and waits for it to take, because a man raised on this soil’s sutras does not begin a thing without the smoke. His hand is steady. Under the sleeve the beads have not moved once since the muster began.
bidam: A woman cannot rule well. / 女主不能善理 — the room said it the year she was crowned and pretended it was weather. / Today we stop pretending.
yumjong: Open the Radiance gate. / High Councillor Bidam comes — today it is the banner, not courtesy.
Before noon Alchun is summoned twice — once by the Sword of Silla, once by the High Councillor with a banner — and he answers both.
alchun: Yushin… / Of course we all loved the princess as young Hwarang. She was a beautiful princess, and we were young men. / But those days are over now. / You need to judge what is best for the nation — and the nation demands that you not be blinded by your personal loyalties, and judge what is best for the divine nation.
alchun: Bidam… / You swore allegiance to the Hwarang, and the divine nation has vested you with the authority of the High Councillor — the highest office in the land. / For you to take up arms against the crown would be an act of highest treason.
alchun: I will not raise a blade against Bidam. / I will not raise a banner against Her Majesty. / Ask me again on the tenth day. I may still be a coward — but I will be a precise one.
Neither man answers him in a way that would satisfy a clerk. Yushin stares at the eastern palace. Bidam smiles as if treason were a word invented by cowards. Alchun walks back to the space between the camps and eats alone.
## DAY 2
Night. Between the camps a small pavilion goes up, open on every side. No chairs. Only a low wooden table. No banner on the ridgepole. Tea already poured. A half moon in an empty sky. They meet the way they used to after sparring: gloves off, courtesy on.
bidam: Yushin. / Tea first. / …When the Six Elders raised Surabol — Lee, Choi, Jeong, Son, Bae, Seol. / Park came from an egg. / There was no Kim.
yushin: …And?
bidam: And now the two Kim houses inside this wall — / Surabol Kim, Alji Kim — / both imports. / I alone… am Six-Elder blood.
The tea cools between them. Neither man drinks enough to call it peace. Bidam smiles as if nothing ugly had been said — the same smile he wore when he crowned a woman king. Yushin sets his cup down unfinished.
Three Hwarang. One princess. The yard remembers what the Council never wrote down.
[FLASHBACK 615 The cleverest of the three]
  Bidam, Alchun, and Yushin — same Hwarang line, same bruised knuckles, same impossible orbit around Princess Dukman. They do not say the word love. The gyuku field says it for them, badly.
  bidam: If the Sacred Bone runs out of men, pick the cleverest woman. / I have known Dukman since we were children. Cleverness is not a gender.
  yushin: Well stood. / Tomorrow on the yard — the hundred-and-ninth is mine.
  alchun: You two will kill each other over a score. / I will kill myself over the girl in the middle. / …That was a joke. File it as a joke.
  Nobody writes down that Bidam’s hall shares blood-whisper with the great Sadaham — the Hwarang who conquered Gaya and refused a slave girl as prize. The chronicle only lets the resemblance show in the jaw, and in the way Bidam treats victory as something that must stay clean.
  Even their names take sides. Bidam’s sounds like this soil and its sutras. Chunchu’s is a foreign classic. Any clerk across the sea could file it without asking. Nobody notices yet. Names are patient.
  bidam: Yushin. / Alchun. / If either of you ever makes her cry for a small reason — I will even the score on your face.
## DAY 3
Arrows trade; messengers lie; the Harmony Council discovers it can convene without deciding anything, which is its highest form. Chunchu’s clerks call the unanimity rule quaint. Bidam calls it ours.
Third night. Same pavilion. Same half moon. Bidam has brought a map — not of the siege, of the roads west.
bidam: Samhan is being colonized — in blood, and in the mind. / Tang sends institutions. India sends… / …through Queen Heo’s blood, sutras. / Yushin — your eyes are handsome. They are a western colour. / …When I stood first, they called me the liberal.
yushin: Gaya blood came from the west too. / I… stood up. / Fifteen winters past, when you spoke — you told me to stand.
bidam: That was when you were weak. / …A joke. Drink your tea.
On the wall Bidam looks west and remembers a cleaner war — Jade Gate Valley, when the enemy still had the courtesy to be foreign.
[FLASHBACK 636 Jade Gate Valley · 옥문곡]
  Baekje sends five hundred armoured men to slip through a valley in the dark. Their job is to bite a fortress from behind. The queen hears about it from a pond of toads. She sends steel instead of prayers.
  alchun: Bidam — left ridge. I take the dry creek. / If Uso loosens a saddle, we do not wait for a committee.
  bidam: Finally — an enemy I am allowed to hate in public. / Alchun. On my mark.
  They fall on the Baekje camp at dusk. Uso climbs a boulder and empties a quiver; the quiver ends before the argument does. Alchun takes the general. Bidam takes the valley’s silence.
  alchun: We make a good pair when the target is outside the wall. / Inside the wall… we will see.
  bidam: Inside the wall is still the sacred country. / I do not miss.
  Eleven years later, on Radiance’s rampart, Bidam will remember Okmun-gok as the last time Alchun stood on his side without hesitating.
Before the fourth night’s tea, Wolseong tries a quieter weapon. Chunchu sends Bupmin (21) to the steam — the water that shows a man’s inner conscience, the past that is driving his hand. Yushin is told only to keep him talking.
chunchu: Bupmin. / Take a jar. / The spring is a place your uncle knows. You’re a Kim — the door will open. / Splash him.
munmu: Father… / What does the water do to a man… / I understand. I’ll go.
This is the first time the cavern goddesses meet Bupmin. He is twenty-one. He does not yet have a king’s name. He has a jar and Chunchu’s weather.
narim: A Kim. / Sit. No — the jar first. / You… He is the best of both. Gaya in the shoulders. Surabol in the mouth. Golhwa is going to climb you if you stay standing. Sit.
golhwa: Oh. / A Kim we haven’t had. He’s both. / Take the water. Conscience sticks to it. Trauma. Grudge. Whatever’s driving the hand. / …And stop standing like that.
golhwa: I’m trying to be a hill and you are shaped like a problem I want in my lap.
hyulle: …Be careful. / If you splash it, you see why he’s doing it. / If you don’t see anything… that’s its own answer. / …He’s pretty. I’ll be quiet. I won’t be calm.
munmu: Goddesses… / Thank you. I was only— / I’ll just take the water.
He fills the jar. He does not stay for the lake’s other lessons. He is the best of both, and he leaves because his father told him to.
## DAY 4
Wolseong’s wells drop. Rumour rises to replace them. Chunchu files contingency letters the way other men file prayers.
Fourth night. Same low table under the half moon. Bidam reads a rumoured draft — never enough secretariat, never enough emperor. His voice stays pleasant. The sentences do not.
bidam: What Chunchu wants… / is a country that fits inside a Tang envelope. / Central rule. Emperor. Clerks. / He would burn the Harmony Council’s unanimity — the one thing we kept.
yushin: Baekje comes with swords, not sentences.
bidam: Yes — and that is why you always win. / On the yard, and here. / Effort… speaks louder than my blood. / …The year they crowned her, I was the liberal who stood for the woman king. / Now they call me the blood-and-soil man. Ironic, Yushin?
yushin: …That young Hwarang is still here.
bidam: Where?
He folds the rumoured draft. The next sentences have been waiting in the sleeve all night.
bidam: Princess Seungman, and the tyranny of Kim Chunchu — I stand against both. / He speaks of a thousand-year kingdom. / If his faction wins, Samhan will spend those thousand years as a Chinese vassal. / A country that never again turns its own wheel.
yushin: With these reforms, under Princess Seungman’s guidance — / a few harvests more, and Silla may stand first in Samhan. / First, even, in all of Haedong — 해동, the East.
bidam: I do not need the strongest nation. / I want neighbours who still know one another’s names. / The young lifting the old. / A true people — not strangers who happen to share a wall.
yushin: The people’s livelihood hangs on the nation’s fullness. / Fullness hangs on institutions — on a government that can still stand. / If Silla falls behind Baekje and Goryeo, what comes through the pass is spear and famine. / Then tell me how the neighbours keep their names.
bidam: Yushin. / Do you — does the royal house — know how common people live? / Have the princesses, or even Chunchu, spent so much as one year beyond the capital? / I have. / Surabol is scarcely ten square miles, ringed by the true Silla. / While we argue here, the common people — the real Sillans — have no wish to live under a foreign emperor’s yoke.
yushin: Surabol is where Hyukgosé was crowned. / Where the Six Elders laid this country’s first stone. / How, then, is Surabol not the real Silla? / As for standing outside — Lord Bidam, I will forever be more outsider than you. / You, of Six-Elder blood, speak so poorly of the halls that raised this land — / while I, last son of a conquered kingdom, am prepared to defend it with my life.
Yushin does not close the argument. He asks again about the pass, about names, about harvests — anything that keeps Bidam’s back to the dark. Behind the 정자, Bupmin’s jar ticks once against a post.
yushin: Bidam. / That ten-mile story. Once more. / The people have no wish for an emperor — where did you hear that.
Bupmin comes from behind to splash the water. It is ugly and precise — cavern water as a hard sheet across Bidam’s shoulders, beads and all.
bidam: Ha… / What is this…
munmu: Your trauma…. / Yushin… why isn’t it doing anything…?
Nothing rises. No childhood. No princess. No grudge-film in the steam. The water runs off the black robe as if it had mistaken a man for a wound. Chunchu, at the pavilion’s edge, does not move. The stoic act holds; the eyes do not.
chunchu: ……
bidam: Oh… haha… / I’ve heard of this… this is that water, isn’t it…?
bidam: HAHAHAHAHA!
bidam: Behold, the arrogance of the sacred bone class!! / You really thought I had to have some sort of personal trauma?? / That that was the reason I was doing all of this? / That I hated the princess? The queen? / That I hated you, Chunchu, or Yushin? / Have you ever… even for a SECOND… considered the POSSIBILITY… / that your ideas are simply terrible? / That they’ll lead this nation to ruin? / That ANY reasonable man would oppose them? / Or are you so ARROGANT to assume… that EVERYTHING you lot do is correct… / and that the ONLY reason for ANYONE to disagree… is because they were suffering some sort of mental disease? Because they were angry and bitter? / Ha… well, my friends, I’m afraid all you’ve done tonight is prove your point. / You’ve proven yourself to be unworthy of leading any country. / So please… my friends… step aside…!
Alchun, arriving late with a lamp, goes pale. An officer asks whether to seize the jar. Nobody answers. Bidam is still laughing, and still alive, and the beads are still counting.
chunchu: If Bidam wins, the Secretariat becomes a quaint hobby. / If Bidam loses, we still have a dying queen and a Tang-shaped hole in the west. / The man would burn a good idea for arriving in a Tang envelope. That is the whole platform — and it polls well. / Munhee — pack for either weather.
munhee: I already packed. / I packed the year the Queen was crowned. You only notice in sieges.
Alchun eats alone between the camps. Both sides send him wine. He drinks neither. Surabol will later call it treason with better stationery.
## DAY 5
Fifth night — the pavilion again. They sit on the floor, alone, the way they used to meet on the training ground. The tea is cold before anyone raises a blade.
yushin: Second Blade of Samhan — Bidam!! Lay down your arms and give your loyalty back to the Blue Moon!!
For a breath they are only the old score again — one hundred and eight to one hundred and eight — two boys who never let the other keep a lead. Then Bidam speaks, and the yard is gone.
bidam: Yushin. / In this country the smartest people hate this country, / and the most patriotic people… are all stupid. / That’s Silla. / The country you’re trying to sell.
bidam: Yushin…. / And besides — you… / you were never even of Silla…!
bidam: Blood is inevitable.
The tea has not been touched. He says it like a compliment that curdled — still the gentleman, still the black robe, still the voice that once shielded this same man from the yard.
yushin: Lord Bidam… I remember we swore our lives to this together…
bidam: You never had a country of your own — selling this one must cost you nothing… / But we are different. We cannot be cut from this land… / Would you hand the country my ancestors built to an emperor…! / I am a son of the sacred country.
yushin: Selling — I have sold nothing. / Lord Chunchu only asks that we learn Tang’s institutions. Baekje comes with swords, not sentences.
bidam: Chunchu — 春秋. The man is named after a Chinese book. / And you would let him write the sacred country’s tomorrow. / Learn another country’s institutions long enough — and one morning, the learning is all that is left.
bidam: I will raise the sacred country’s glory again, / I will return the sacred country’s future to its own people!
[FLASHBACK 618 One hundred and eight]
  The yard after rain. Two Hwarang, neither willing to leave the mud with the score uneven.
  bidam: One hundred and seven…! / Brother — today I take the lead!
  yushin: One hundred and eight. / Get up. An uneven number does not sleep.
  bidam: Ha! / Afraid it will be written that Gaya blood lost to Silla blood?
  yushin: Written or not. / I am still your elder brother. / Again.
  They end the evening even. They always do.
“You were never even of Silla.” To see where that began, we go back to a Gaya prince nobody names…!

=== EPISODE 43: Muryuk (562) [flashback]
For five hundred years the people of Gaya lived by iron and by six eggs, and they enjoyed great peace.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Jinheung, yr. 23 (562), 9th month; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 98] In the ninth month Gaya rebelled. The king ordered Isabu to punish them, with Sadaham as deputy. Isabu brought up the army, and they all surrendered at once.
The Cloud King and his boy-general Sadaham come for Gaya.
sadaham: They said too young. / The gate didn’t.
mugwan: Don’t die first.
sadaham: Then keep up.
The vanguard thought otherwise. After the city fell he opened the prize-cages and kept only Alcheon dirt. Take the land. Leave the people.
sadaham: Alcheon dirt. / That’s enough.
Thirty years earlier, another Gaya prince had already handed his kingdom over. His name was Muryuk. His grandson will be Kim Yushin. But before the hall, the field. The tall Gaya cone still fights.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 4, Silla Annals — King Beopheung, yr. 19 (532); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 86] The lord of Geumgwan, Kim Guhae, came with his queen and three sons, bringing the treasury and precious things of the country, and surrendered.
muryuk: If I am to surrender, I have one condition… / Let my sons live in Silla without shame…
jinheung: And what do you mean by that?
muryuk: In Silla… I know a man’s blood decides everything… / Sacred Bone, True Bone… I know it all… / If my descendants — the sons and daughters of Suro and Heo — can take a worthy place… / then I too am ready to give Silla my life…
jinheung: Very well. Your descendants shall be raised as True Bones of Silla.
Three generations later, his grandson will still be told he is not really one of them.
muryuk: Your grace is boundless… Your Majesty…!
muryuk: Yushin…
Back to the siege. Sixth night. Bidam has poured two cups of tea. Yushin isn't coming… is he?

=== EPISODE 44: Jeon (轉) (647)
## DAY 6
Night rain. Bidam’s officers want a dawn assault. Bidam wants the score finished properly. He wants Yushin to come out again.
Sixth night. Yushin does not come to the pavilion. Bidam sends tea anyway — two cups poured, one left steaming.
bidam: …He is not coming today. / Very well. Courtesy held until the sixth night.
[FLASHBACK 612 The headband]
  The Hwarang hall, the new boy’s first day. Two seniors lean across his desk.
  Senior Hwarang: So he isn’t even a real True Bone!
  bidam: Hey, enough! / What did any of you do to earn True Bone? / You were merely born into it.
  yushin: Thank you.
  bidam: What is there to thank? / Take this headband. Keep it, and no one will trouble you.
Sixth night. The cup Yushin did not drink sits where Bidam left it. Courtesy held — and then, under the half moon, does not.
Near midnight Yushin comes to the pavilion after all. He does not touch the cup.
bidam: You Gaya wretch…! / You dare call yourself the sacred country’s saviour….
yushin: Lord Bidam. / Fifteen years past, in the Harmony Council — who was it that stood up for Princess Dukman?
bidam: ……
yushin: That young Hwarang said he would choose the cleverest of the three. / Where did that man go, Lord Bidam?
bidam: …That man lived back when the sacred country was still a country.
yushin: But it is not I who raised a banner against the sacred country…!
## DAY 7
## Not a Kim
Bidam finds the cavern the way a man finds a rumor. Sword on the lip. Beads in the fist. The navy coat comes off because he has heard Yushin wash here, and a man who wants what Yushin has will copy the wash if he cannot copy the name.
He walks into the steam with nothing on but water and one hundred and eight beads.
The three sisters are already on the far rock. Narim looks at him the way an eldest looks at a door that opened wrong.
Golhwa’s invitation is not meant for him, and she is wet anyway; the steam does not care whose body it is until the name is wrong.
The spring does not hide much. Heat hits him low. He is already rock-hard in the black bowl before he has finished looking, and the waterline he is using as a wall is doing the opposite of hiding him. He recites. The beads do not help.
I came to wash. The sutra does not cover this. I am standing in a door I cannot close.
The beads stop mid-count. He stares. The waterline drops.
golhwa: Wrong door. He brought iron. And that.
narim: He is not a Kim. The steam already knows.
hyulle: …The mouth. Before the water takes the blade.
They do not stay women.
Golhwa goes first — fire unfolding into a tiger the size of the rock, ember pelt, steam off the fangs. Hyullé’s silk becomes a water-serpent, long as the bowl, cyan scales. Narim’s elder-shape thickens into a moss-bear, leaves in the fur, the hill’s weight on four feet.
He recoils. The beads jump. The sword is a hard black line he cannot lift in time.
They kick him toward the light — tiger-shoulder, serpent-coil, bear-shove. Three beasts, one refusal. The night has him again. The lake keeps Kims. It does not keep slogans.
## The Lake, Again
On the seventh night Yushin goes to the cavern lake, as if habit could hold a country together.
Yushin undresses without ceremony. The three are already in the steam — mentors, tormentors, the only room in Silla where no one asks him for a victory.
Golhwa knows that walk and is already wet for it. The spring hides nothing; he is hard before he has finished looking, and he pretends the water is arithmetic while Golhwa watches him like a problem she means to solve with her body.
golhwa: You came early. How flattering.
narim: He came because he is about to kill a friend. / Forest etiquette: say it plain.
yushin: If you know that, tell me how not to.
hyulle: You can’t. / …I’m sorry. / Keep the wound that remembers the headband. Lose the one that wants him to thank you for the blade.
golhwa: Unless you’re saving all your thank-yous for the Queen again. / She is not in the water, Yushin. We are.
She takes his wrist under the water and does not wait for the Queen’s name to finish. For a few breaths there is only steam, and the walk they already know, and a marshal who cannot keep his arithmetic. Then Narim’s voice cuts the wick.
yushin: But Her Majesty —
narim: Enough, fire. / He will go. We knew that when he took the armour off and still kept her name on.
hyulle: …Go. / Give Sunduk the victory. / Keep a little silence for us.
Steam thins. Two shapes wait where the rock shelves into black: the father who taught him that loyalty is soil, and the grandfather who traded a kingdom so a grandson could keep a sword.
yushin: Father. Grandfather. / In six days the same mouth has called me the sacred country’s saviour and a Gaya wretch. / Which of the two do I carry out to the tenth morning?
seohyeon: Yushin, my beloved son. / You were the light of my life, and now the nation needs you to be its savior. / I am sorry that I was not of Silla blood… I tried my hardest to forget my Gaya roots, and tried to pretend that I was something I was not. / But you don’t need to do that anymore. / Son, you are the mighty Sword of Silla, and the Last Prince of Gaya. / But you are infinitely more than that…! / You are my son. You are Kim Yushin. / Your mother and I couldn’t be more proud of you…!
muryuk: Yushin, my beloved grandson. / When I swore allegiance to the Silla crown, it was not for my own sake, but for yours. / I loved you before I knew you. / Yushin, look at me. / I am so, so proud of you…!
yushin: Father… / Grandfather… / Thank you.
golhwa: Look at him — he’s crying.
## DAY 8
On the eighth night a star falls toward Wolseong — bright enough that both camps look up. Bidam does not invent the omen. He only names it in a useful direction.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Bidam’s rebellion, 647)] I have heard that where a star falls, blood will surely be shed. This is likely an omen that the woman sovereign will be defeated.
bidam: You heard it. / Heaven has already voted against a woman on the throne. / 女主不能善理 — and now the sky writes it in fire.
The rebel shout shakes the ground. Inside Wolseong Queen Sunduk goes pale. Yushin asks for leave to speak — and for a kite, a torch, and enough lies to edit heaven.
yushin: Your Majesty — do not fear a falling light. / If they can read a star, they can also unread one.
He flies the kite from the palace dark: a burning scarecrow rising where the star had fallen, so the night sky seems to take its light back.
yushin: Look up. / Heaven changed its mind — or we changed heaven’s handwriting. / Hwarang, with me.
The kite buys one night. A sky can only be argued with for so long, and by the grey hour both camps are already arguing about what they saw. Before the drums, Yushin goes down to the palace stables alone and leads out the white horse.
Hangyul has carried him for eighteen years, since the charge at Nangbi Fortress, to every border the queen sent him to and a few he went to without asking. The groom, a boy of fourteen, works out what the rope in the marshal’s other hand is for before anyone says it, and starts to cry with his mouth shut.
[FLASHBACK 612 Hanbyul]
  Seventeen, drunk, and asleep in the saddle. His first horse, Hanbyul, does what any good horse does with a sleeping rider and takes him where he always goes. He wakes at the courtesan Cheongwan’s gate with her lantern already lifted and her face already glad.
  cheongwan: You came? / …They said you swore to your mother you’d never come again.
  He had sworn it. The horse had not. He gets down, draws, and takes Hanbyul’s head off at the gate in one stroke, then walks home past the lantern without looking at it. The song Cheongwan made about that night outlives both of them.
The star came down past the west wall of Wolseong, where the ground is still scorched in a long smear. Yushin walks Hangyul there himself. Chunchu is already waiting with two priests, a bronze basin, and a face that has decided not to argue.
chunchu: …There are other white horses. Three in the stable. / Does it have to be this one?
yushin: They know over there. Everyone knows which horse I ride. / Offer someone else’s horse and it isn’t heaven that laughs. It’s Bidam.
He takes the halter off with his own hands. Hangyul, who has been led to a great many strange places at night, puts his nose into Yushin’s chest and waits for the reason, as he always has.
yushin: Eighteen years. / If it weren’t for you at Nangbi, I’d have ended there. / …I’m sorry. This time I’m the one who brought you.
chunchu: Yushin. / …Want me to do it?
yushin: No. / He’s mine.
He does it the way the rite asks and faster than the rite asks, so the horse never quite finishes turning his head. White goes down into the scorched black. The priests begin the prayer, and Yushin, who has never once let another man finish a sentence for him, lets them.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biographies — Kim Yushin; Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 2 (Bidam’s rebellion, 647)] He slaughtered a white horse and offered it at the place where the star had fallen, and prayed: “In the way of Heaven, yang is firm and yin is yielding; in the way of men, the sovereign is honoured and the subject humble. Should this ever be reversed, there is great disorder.”
Across the field, on the Radiance wall, Bidam watches the smoke of the offering go up and asks an officer what was burned. When he is told, he puts his beads away for the first time in eight days and goes down to the lines to stand beside his own horse, Bisamun, for a while, saying nothing to anybody.
At dawn the groom leads out a young grey, too green for a marshal, the only horse left in the royal stable that nobody has been afraid of all week.
yushin: Name?
The boy shakes his head. He is still crying.
yushin: Hanseul. / …It’s easy to say. Stop crying and try it.
It is the last horse he names. He rides Hanseul out on the tenth day, and across the Yellow Mountain fields thirteen years later, and never once lets a groom catch him brushing it longer than the others.
## DAY 9
Assault and counter-assault. Yumjong falls in the outer works — the quieter name on the banner, gone first. Bidam does not. By dusk the granary inside Wolseong is down to its last sacks, and men who have never prayed are learning the postures. Alchun is asked, for the last useful time, which wall he belongs to.
alchun: I belong to the country that survives the week. / If that answer is empty — then so is the chair you will offer me afterward.
He still does not draw. After Bidam falls, Surabol will remember that sentence for years — the man who caught tigers, filed under Neither.
That night, on Radiance’s rampart, Bidam speaks — to his officers, to the wall, to whichever chronicler is still awake. They expect a battle plan. They get a confession.
bidam: You know… we call this country the “sacred country.” But our country isn’t the greatest in the world. / Its kings are not the most wise. Its armies are not the strongest. / Its men are not the most noble. Its women are not the most chaste. / Our natural scenery is beautiful, but there are more beautiful sights elsewhere. / For every good thing our nation has, there are other nations with greater things.
bidam: However — that is not why we call it the sacred country.
bidam: We call it the sacred country, because it is ours. / Because our kings rule over our people. Because our armies are composed of our sons. / Because our men get up every day, and try to make the next day better. / Because our women go to sleep every night, knowing that they have raised our next generation with our blood and our seed. / Because our hills and rivers are the ones that we have grown up with as children — where we used to play with our fathers, and where we will play with our sons.
bidam: That is what I am defending.
bidam: The crown may call me a traitor, a heretic, an old man who needs to adapt to the times… / …and to all of that, I simply say no. / I don’t need to say any more than that.
bidam: And one day, our descendants will prove me right. / So come at me, fate! Bidam is ready to defend what is ours.
Never of Silla? Then where did Yushin come from? Fifty years back: a Gaya boy, a royal gate, and a lost horse…!

=== EPISODE 45: Seohyun (593) [flashback]
Before there is a Yushin there is a road, and a young man on it who should be looking where he is going.
Kim Seohyeon is the son of Gaya’s last prince. In the capital, that’s the kind of fact people bring up just after he leaves the room. His father handed the kingdom over, then spent his life proving it had been a bargain. On one road he took an enemy king, four generals and ten thousand heads. The family is True Bone now. The rank opens most doors in the capital. It opens the best ones least.
He is young and polite and so used to being the Gaya boy in the room that he apologises before anyone has accused him of anything. He sits a horse better than he sits a banquet.
The best gate on the street belongs to Sukhuljong, the great king’s younger brother. Royal on every side. His daughter Manmyung is standing in it when Seohyeon rides past. He looks. The histories, which don’t usually notice such things, record exactly how.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] At first, Seohyeon saw on the road Manmyung, daughter of Sukhuljong, son of Galmun-wang Ipjong. His heart was glad, and he courted her with his eyes; and without waiting for a go-between, they came together.
## The Gate
The first time, he looks and keeps riding and nearly puts his horse into a charcoal cart. The second time he has an errand ready at the far end of the street, which does not exist. By the third the errand has run out, and he is only a man on a horse going the wrong way slowly.
Manmyung’s maid: Agassi. It’s him again. / Same horse. Same— he’s pretending he isn’t looking.
manmyung: He’s terrible at it. / Don’t look. …No, look. I want to see what he does.
Then she does something nobody on that street has seen a Sacred Bone daughter do. She steps down off the threshold into the dust.
manmyung: You’ve ridden past this gate three times today. / Is the road that bad, or are you lost?
seohyeon: I— the horse— / …It’s lost. I’m only on it.
manmyung: It looked fine the first time. / Nearly ate a charcoal cart. But fine.
seohyeon: That was— the cart was in the wrong— / Kim Seohyeon. That’s— I should have said that first. Is it rude? I don’t know the rule for this.
manmyung: There isn’t one. That’s why it’s fun. / And I know who you are. Everyone on this street knows who you are.
seohyeon: …Ah. / The Gaya one.
manmyung: The one with the nice horse. / Then let it get lost again tomorrow. Same hour.
Manmyung’s maid: Agassi—!
## Getting Lost
It gets lost every day for a season. The maid starts timing her errands by it. The charcoal man learns to pull over. Nobody sends a matchmaker, because a matchmaker would have to walk into Sukhuljong’s hall and say the word Gaya out loud.
By the end of summer they have stopped pretending about the horse. He leaves it at the bottom of the lane and walks up, and she talks to him through the side gate with the bar still down, because a gate with the bar down is technically closed.
manmyung: You’re late. / The horse?
seohyeon: The horse is fine. The horse is better than me. / They kept us at the Ministry. There’s talk of a posting.
manmyung: Where?
seohyeon: They haven’t said. North, probably. They send Gaya men north. / Somewhere with a lot of Goguryeo and not much—
manmyung: Not much me.
seohyeon: …I was going to say not much rice.
manmyung: Liar.
The posting comes in the autumn: governor of Manno, a county far up the Goguryeo road, a wooden wall and a granary and a great many hills that change hands. He comes to the side gate with the seal still in his sleeve.
seohyeon: Manno. / It’s— a long way. Ten days if the passes are open. The house is small. I haven’t seen it, but they said small, and the way they said it— / I’m asking badly. I’m asking if you would—
manmyung: Yes.
seohyeon: —come with— I haven’t finished.
manmyung: Then finish. It’s still yes.
The maid tells nobody. The charcoal man tells everybody. Her father knows by the next morning.
## Sukhuljong’s Hall
Sukhuljong takes the news sitting down, the way he takes most things, without looking up from his cup. He is a king’s son and a king’s brother, and he has never once in his life been the one left standing.
sukhuljong: Muryuk’s boy. / The one whose father carried his country here in a box and set it on the floor in front of my brother. / Him?
manmyung: His father kept his sword, Father. / You keep a gate.
sukhuljong: A Gaya chair in a Kim hall. / Every guest who came would sit on it just to hear it creak. / Then you can look at the gate from the inside.
manmyung: You can’t keep me in a room forever.
sukhuljong: I don’t need forever. / I need until he leaves for Manno.
He shuts her in a house apart at the back of the compound and sets men on the door. Surabol has a word for what the two of them did, and it is not a polite one, and for a few weeks it is the only thing the city talks about.
## The House Apart
The guards are two cousins off one of Sukhuljong’s farms, chosen because they cannot be bribed and cannot read, and by the fourth night they have run out of things to say to each other.
First guard: You think he’ll come?
Second guard: The Gaya one? He says sorry to his own horse. / He’s not coming over a wall.
First guard: I heard he leaves for the north day after tomorrow. First light.
Second guard: Good. Then we go home.
Inside, Manmyung has stopped eating to make a point and started again because the point was only hurting her. She has counted the boards in the ceiling. At the foot of the back wall, where the drain runs out, there is a gap, and she has been looking at it for three days the way her father looks at furniture.
On the last night it storms. Lightning comes down on the door itself, and the guards do what men do when the sky picks out the house they are guarding, which is run. In the noise Manmyung goes out through a gap in the wall so low that she has to crawl, in her good silk, in the mud.
Second guard: Heaven— it hit the door, it hit the DOOR—
First guard: Leave it! It’s burning, leave the door, leave it—
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] Seohyeon was made governor of Manno commandery and meant to take her with him. Only then did Sukhuljong learn that his daughter had come together with Seohyeon outside the rites. He hated it, shut her in a separate house, and set men to guard it. Suddenly lightning struck the door of the house; the guards scattered in terror; Manmyung got out through a hole in the wall and went with Seohyeon to Manno.
He is at the bottom of the lane with two horses, because he has been there every one of the four nights, in case. He sees a shape come out of the drain on its elbows, stand up and walk toward him through the rain like a woman going to market.
manmyung: Don’t— don’t look at the dress. / Is the horse lost tonight?
seohyeon: You— the lightning— are you hurt? Your hands—
manmyung: My hands are fine. Answer the question.
seohyeon: …No. / Tonight it knows exactly where it’s going.
They ride north in the rain. Behind them, two cousins are trying to explain a door to Sukhuljong.
## Manno
Manno is a wooden wall, a granary, a county office with a leaking roof, and hills that have changed hands more often than the clerks can keep up with. She learns the granary. He learns the hills. Neither of them learns to cook, and by the second month the clerk’s wife has taken pity on them.
He has a dream on a gyeongjin night and tells nobody for three weeks, because a Gaya man who dreams of stars coming down on him does not say so in a county office. Then, on a sinchuk night, she sits up in the dark and shakes him.
manmyung: Wake up. Wake up, I had— there was a boy. / In gold. Armour, all gold. He came in on a cloud, right into the hall, through the door like he owned the house. He looked at me.
seohyeon: …I had one too. Three weeks ago. / Two stars. A red one and a yellow one. They came down on me. Not on the house. On me.
manmyung: Three weeks. / Stars fell on you and you didn’t tell me for three weeks.
seohyeon: I thought it might be the soup.
manmyung: Pfft— the soup— / Come here, you. Come here.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] On the night of a gyeongjin day Seohyeon dreamed that the two stars Mars and Saturn came down upon him; and Manmyung, on the night of a sinchuk day, dreamed that a boy clad in golden armour rode a cloud into the hall. Soon she was with child, and after twenty months she gave birth to Yushin.
She is with child by spring. She is still with child the following spring, and the clerk’s wife, who has delivered half the county, stops coming to check and starts coming to stare.
The clerk’s wife: Twenty months, my lady. / I’ve had cows do it faster. / Either that child is something, or somebody counted wrong at the start, and I won’t say which. You’re the governor’s.
manmyung: Say it. I want to hear you say it.
The clerk’s wife: …The child’s something.
The boy is born in the county house at Manno. The clerk’s wife turns him over to wash him. She stops with the cloth in her hand.
The clerk’s wife: My lady. His back. / Look— there. There’s seven. Like someone pressed them in with a thumb.
seohyeon: Seven what?
The clerk’s wife: Stars, sir. The Dipper. On a baby. / I’m going to sit down.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Marvels — Kim Yushin] Lord Yushin was born in the eulmyo year, the seventeenth of King Jinpyeong. He was endowed with the essence of the Seven Luminaries, and so his back bore a pattern of seven stars; and there were many other wonders about him.
Naming him takes longer than carrying him did.
seohyeon: Gyeongjin. / I want to call him for the night I dreamed. That’s where he came from.
manmyung: You can’t name a child after a day. / Even I know that, and I ran away from all my tutors.
seohyeon: I know. I know. / But gyeong, written down, looks like yu. And jin, said quickly, is nearly sin. / And there was a man in the old books. A scholar. Yu Xin. A good man, they say. / So it isn’t a day. It’s a scholar. Nobody can say anything.
manmyung: You’ve been working on this for months.
seohyeon: …Twenty.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] When it came to choosing a name, he said to his wife: “I had a lucky dream on the gyeongjin night and got this child; it would be right to name him for it. But the rites do not allow a name from a day or a month. Now, gyeong 庚 resembles yu 庾 in writing, and jin 辰 is close to sin 信 in sound; what is more, there was a worthy of old named Yu Xin. Why not name him that?” So he was named Yushin.
They bury the afterbirth on the high hill behind the county, the way you do with a child you mean to keep, and the hill keeps the name.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] Yushin’s placenta was buried on a high hill, and to this day it is called Taeryeong, the Mountain of the Placenta Spirit.
manmyung: Yushin. / Say it to my father, next time you’re in Surabol. Say it at his gate.
seohyeon: …He won’t open it.
manmyung: Then say it louder.
## The Name at the Gate
A few weeks after the birth he rides to Surabol and says the name at Sukhuljong’s gate, loudly, to a street that has stopped to listen. The gate does not open. A steward comes out instead.
Sukhuljong’s steward: His lordship is unwell. / He expects to be unwell for some years. He asked me to say it in exactly those words.
seohyeon: Tell him— / Tell him the boy has his mother’s mouth. / He’ll know what that means.
Sukhuljong’s steward: …I’ll tell him, sir. / He won’t like it.
## The Spring
He rides home the long way because he does not want to arrive yet. The road goes over a ridge beyond the city that nobody uses, and by noon he wants water more than he has ever wanted a shrine. When heat breathes out of the hillside he calls it a spring and gets down.
Under the hill three sisters keep the heat in the stone, the water in the dark and the moss on the roots: Golhwa, Hyullé, and Narim, the eldest, who also keeps the rules. They have gone centuries without a man coming down to them, and the hill has just told them about hooves on the road.
golhwa: Hooves! Unni. Unni, hooves. Someone stopped.
narim: Someone always stops. They drink, they piss in the stream, they leave.
hyulle: …This one’s crying a little.
golhwa: Crying? Let me see— move your elbow—
golhwa: Fox. Let’s be a fox. Foxes are fun.
hyulle: A grandmother. Then he drinks and bows and goes, and nobody… nobody gets hurt.
narim: Try both. Then I pick.
They try both. The fox frightens the horse. The grandmother makes him kneel and offer her his waterskin with both hands, which is so polite that Golhwa groans out loud through the rock. Narim picks the last face herself: three young women in white jeogori over moss-green and ember and pale water-blue, sitting on the far rock as if they had always been there.
He is still calling it a spring when the ground gives under his boot. He comes down through warm dark into a bowl of black water under stone and stands up coughing in a cloud of steam, soaked to the skin, his sword still somehow in his hand.
seohyeon: Who— forgive me— who lives here? / I was looking for water. There was an old woman just now, up there—
hyulle: …That was me. Sorry.
narim: You found your water. All of it at once. / Put the sword down, please. You’ll cut the steam.
golhwa: Hi. I’m Golhwa. That’s unni. That’s Hyullé, she won’t say hello unless you look at her first. / What’s your name? Say it slow.
seohyeon: Kim. Kim Seohyeon. / Are you… I mean. People?
At the surname all three of them go quiet. Kim is the sound their own steam makes coming off the water, and nobody has ever said it to them as a name.
golhwa: Kim. / Say it again. No, I heard you. It just… sticks.
narim: Kim. / …Then the house rules apply. Golhwa. Chin.
Golhwa is across the pool before he can step back, a wet hand under his jaw, turning his face to the light like a horse trader.
golhwa: Smooth. Shaved this morning? For who— oh. For the gate. Poor thing. / Chin passes, unni.
narim: Second rule. Nobody stands in this water dressed. / The steam doesn’t talk to cloth.
seohyeon: I— I have a wife. She’s— we have a son, he’s— / I’m sorry. I should have said that first.
golhwa: We didn’t ask about her.
hyulle: …You can turn around. We won’t— we won’t look.
golhwa: Speak for yourself.
He turns his back, takes off the wet clothes and folds them badly on a rock, because he does not know what else to do with his hands. Hyullé does not look, mostly. Golhwa does not pretend. Narim waits until he is in the water to the chest and then lets out a breath, which nobody remarks on.
narim: Today we are the mouths the hill uses when it gets tired of being stone. / Ask it one thing, Kim. From the water. Once.
He thinks of the gate. He thinks of a girl crawling through a hole in a wall in her good silk.
seohyeon: I have a son. A few weeks old. / My wife’s father won’t say his name. I stood at his gate this morning and said it for him, and— / I don’t know what to ask for him. I don’t know what you ask for a boy like that.
Their eyes go solid, green and cyan and ember, and the cave stops being funny.
The Hill: The child will be the measure two countries cannot share. / They will call him a blade and mean a border. / When they say he was never of them, the blade will still be Kim. / He will cut more than he is given. Don’t ask who bleeds.
Narim puts a river stone in his hand, ordinary and grey and too warm for the cave.
narim: Keep it in your sleeve. / When it’s warm, come back. Same road, same water. One question. / When you’re too old to climb, send the boy.
golhwa: Shaved.
seohyeon: …Can I tell his mother?
golhwa: Tell her it was a spring. / Everybody says that.
He rides north with a stone in his sleeve that will not cool. At Manno, Manmyung is sitting up with the baby in the lamplight, and she asks him where he has been all day, and he tells her he found a spring.
manmyung: A spring. / …You’re smiling like a man who found three.
seohyeon: …It was a very good spring.
manmyung: Mm. / Your hair’s wet. It hasn’t rained in a week.
## Fifteen
The boy grows up at the edge of things, in county houses on the northern road. There’s a younger brother, and two little sisters the house calls by baby names. They’ll grow up to cause a great deal of trouble over a skirt. One of them is Munhee.
At fifteen he is made a hwarang, and the boys who follow him start calling themselves the Dragon-Flower Band. Seohyeon hears it from a clerk before he hears it from his son.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] At fifteen the lord became a hwarang. The people of the time followed him gladly, and his band was called the Dragon-Flower Incense Band.
The morning Yushin leaves for Surabol, his father stops him at the gate of the county house to look at his headband.
seohyeon: You’ve got it on crooked.
yushin: It’s fine, Father.
seohyeon: It’s crooked. Hold still. / In Surabol they’ll look at the headband before they look at you. They’ll look for anything.
yushin: Because we’re Gaya.
seohyeon: …Because you’re new. / Mostly because you’re new.
He reties it with both hands, too tight, and then does it a third time. Manmyung watches from the doorway and lets him.
manmyung: Let him go. He’ll be late for his own band.
yushin: Mother—
manmyung: And stop at your grandfather’s gate on the way. / Don’t knock. Just let them see you.
## Daeyang
Seohyeon rises the way a Gaya man rises in the capital. One rank at a time, each signed by someone who remembers the box. By the end he is third rank in the kingdom. He governs the march that faces the enemy, from the fortress at Daeya. His son’s memorial stone will give him a different name. The historian can’t decide between them, writes both down, and moves on.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 41, Biography of Kim Yushin, part 1] His grandfather Muryeok was Commander of the Army of the Sinju Circuit; he once led troops that captured the king of Baekje and four of his generals and took more than ten thousand heads. His father Seohyeon rose to the rank of Sopan, Governor-General of Daeyang Province and Pacifier of all the armies of Daeyang Province.
In the evenings he walks the wall at Daeya. Baekje is a line of hills to the west that the sun goes down behind.
A Daeya officer: They say this wall can’t be taken, sir.
seohyeon: They say that about— every wall, I think. I’ve heard it about four. / Just— keep the granary dry. And know whose hands the keys are in. / My wife ran the granary at Manno. She’d tell you the same. She’d tell you better.
The histories do not record the year he died, only how high he got. He climbs the ridge beyond the city whenever the stone in his sleeve is warm, shaved every time, until the climb is too much for him, and then he sends the name. The boy with seven stars on his back finds the same water forty years after the gate, and the hill knows his walk before he does.
Tenth morning. The grain is gone. Two old yard-mates walk out between the camps, and the score is still a hundred and eight apiece…!

=== EPISODE 46: Gyeol (結) (647)
## DAY 10
Before the gate opens Bidam goes down to the lines and saddles Bisamun himself, which a High Councillor does not do. He slips nine beads off the end of his string and knots them to the bridle, under the horse’s jaw.
?: Sangdaedeung, those are…
bidam: Master Wongwang’s fifth precept. Be choosy about killing. / Never the animals that work for you. Horse, ox, chicken, dog. / …They burned a white horse over there the other day. Even if I lose, somebody should still be holding on to this one.
Bisamun is named for the guardian king who stands at the north of every temple with a pagoda in his hand. Bidam rubs the horse’s nose once and speaks to it in the voice he keeps for sutras.
bidam: You’re named for the one who guards the north. / Today just watch the west.
They meet again between the camps — not as High Councillor and marshal, but as the yard’s two best. Dragon pommel against heavenly horse. The first exchanges are almost gentle. That is how Hwarang kill each other.
Yushin wins the way a man wins when he would rather lose — late, ugly, through a guard he taught Bidam twenty years ago. The heavenly-horse blade drops. Blood finds the mud that used to be a scoreboard.
bidam: …One hundred and nine. / Finally.
Bidam smiles with blood in his teeth — the same boy who once offered a headband across a desk.
bidam: Hwarang Kim Yushin…
Yushin does not move to finish it, and there is nothing left to finish. For as long as the breath lasts the two of them look at each other the way they used to across the yard, back when the score was even and neither one wanted to go home.
The body finishes falling after the name does.
Kangrim reads his name three times where the body has not yet finished falling — Bidam. Bidam. Bidam. — the ledger catching up to the last word.
Bisamun comes through the lines without a rider, at a walk, and stops over him. Nine beads swing under its jaw. When a Silla groom reaches for the bridle it lays its ears flat and shows him its teeth, and the groom, who has had a long ten days, steps back.
yushin: Leave it. / …Let it go. North.
Nobody asks him why north. The horse stands there until the body is taken, then turns and goes, past the Radiance wall and up the valley road, and afterwards the officers on the rampart cannot agree whether anyone opened the gate for it.
Yushin does not kneel. Mud still wet, he turns to the Hwarang behind him and names a house. Bidam’s own line. The one he carried in his jaw and never once claimed aloud.
yushin: Erase Bidam’s house. / The Son line — all Musan, all Gurema’s descendants. / Treason’s blood must be cut.
alchun: Yushin… / Bidam is dead. He poured tea for ten days, then took the blade. / If you burn his hall — we erase one of the Six Elders with our own hands.
Yushin leans close — close enough that the officers hear only breath, and Alchun hears the sentence.
yushin: Blood is inevitable…
Alchun goes pale. Down the line an officer asks for the order to be repeated. Nobody repeats it. Yushin mounts, and the order stands.
kangrim: High Councillor. / Your list ends here. Walk with me — His Majesty’s kingdom keeps better minutes than Surabol.
kangrim: High Councillor — before the minutes close. / The opposite kite. What do you want written?
bidam: …Write that I flew it. / The rest they can guess. / Tell the sacred country I loved it badly.
Bidam falls the way a Hwarang falls — eyes open, form unbroken. The kite burns out over the wall. Somewhere behind Yushin the queen is already slipping away.
Rain finds the lattice before the physicians do. It is a small rain. It beads on the marshal’s sleeve and on the queen’s mouth, and neither of them has a hand free for it.
yushin: Your Majesty.
sunduk: General.
yushin: The physicians are in the corridor. / I told them the rain can wait.
sunduk: Leave them. / It is a small rain. It will not be what takes me.
yushin: Your Majesty—
sunduk: The year I took the crown. You remember. / You said you would serve me to the end.
yushin: “I will serve you to the end.”
sunduk: Yes. / And here we are.
yushin: Did I not promise to stay to the last moment.
sunduk: You did. General.
sunduk: …Princess. / Say it the old way. / When you lost the count on the yard, I was a princess.
yushin: Hwarang. That is what I was. / A hwarang who lost one count.
sunduk: You do not lose counts.
yushin: I lost one. / Which one, I will not say.
sunduk: Then stop being a general about it.
sunduk: Dukman.
yushin: …Don’t.
sunduk: Since the vote I have been Majesty. / Say the name I had before the room.
yushin: Dukman.
sunduk: Yushin.
yushin: I am here.
sunduk: I know. / Stay. / I can do a little rain.
The rain keeps on, small, on the lattice and on his sleeve. Her hand stays in his until it does not. The escort waits until the marshal’s hands have finished their work.
Kangrim reads her name three times — Dukman. Dukman. Dukman. — the ledger’s habit before a Sacred Bone line closes.
That night Yushin remembers the first day of the rebellion, and it is not the way he has been telling it.
[FLASHBACK 612 the twist]
  yushin: It’s all right. I will overcome it myself. / My name is Kim Yushin! I will be the great general of Silla!! / Oh — and your name, hyung?
  bidam: My name? Bidam. / That kid…. he’ll be someone great.
That night Yushin walks out alone to the pavilion between the old camp lines. The low table is still there, and on it the cup he never touched. He sits down across from no one.
[FLASHBACK 647 The sixth night · 여섯째 밤]
  bidam: You Gaya wretch…!
The one hand that said no is gone. Now the crown has to fit Seungman, and it was made for someone else…!

=== EPISODE 47: Queen Jinduk (647)
The crown was made for her cousin and has to be padded at the temples. Seungman sits very still while the goldsmith does it, because somebody told her once that Dukman never fidgeted, and she has believed it for forty years.
Seungman is crowned Queen Jinduk before the blood on the yard dries. The bloodline’s last polite miracle, stamped and filed while the censers are still warm. The succession Bidam died objecting to passes at last. Unanimously.
Alchun is not at the coronation. The court writes his absence down as illness. Everyone understands the illness’s true name: Day 1 through Day 10, unanswered.
The court does not mean to compare. It simply cannot stop. The old Queen read the peony seeds before they were planted. She heard frogs at Jade Gate Pond in midwinter and sent two thousand men to the exact valley where five hundred Baekje soldiers were hiding. She named the day of her own death and was right about it. The new Queen is gentle, and good at a loom, and has never once predicted anything.
courtmaid: The old Queen would have known it was going to rain. / Shh. / …She would have, though.
jinduk: Yushin… preserve the sacred country…
jinduk: Bidam…
jinduk: Yushin… surely Bidam’s words are not weighing on you…?
yushin: No — what could there be to weigh on me. / I am a loyal servant of the sacred country.
jinduk: Chunchu. / Unni knew about the frogs before the frogs did. I can’t even tell when it’s going to rain.
chunchu: Majesty, nobody asks the moon to be the sun. / They love it because it lets them look straight at it.
jinduk: …You had that ready.
chunchu: Since the funeral, Majesty.
At night she sits at a loom, because her hands want work that nobody will compare. Three years from now she will weave an ode to the Tang emperor into a length of silk, and it will do more for Silla than any prophecy her cousin made. Nobody at court thinks to compare that.
Silla needs an army. Only one man alive can lend it. Chunchu goes west…!

=== EPISODE 48: Huangdi (皇帝) (648)
## Shimin & Chunchu
Prince Chunchu (45) approaches the Second Emperor and offers an alliance, vowing revenge against Baekje.
In Chang’an he watches a machine that doesn’t wait for uncles. One office drafts. One checks. One carries it out through six boards. One seal. One speed.
[diagram tang-departments]
The embassy comes in at the hour the street drums stop. The great avenue opens ahead of it, a hundred and fifty paces wide and perfectly empty.
The second banner was lettered, the older clerks say, SERVE THE PEOPLE. But the second character of the people, 民, is also the second character of the emperor’s name, and nobody in Chang’an writes that. The sign-painters found a word of the right width.
chunchu: Inmun. That one over the lodging gate. Read it for me.
inmun: …“The Greater China Co-Prosperity Sphere,” Father.
chunchu: Co-prosperity. Prospering together. A lovely word. / …Odd place to hang it, though. Over the one door where the foreigners sleep.
inmun: I think it’s there for us to read.
chunchu: Then remember it. / When the big house offers to share the harvest, the small house counts its own granary before supper.
Chang’an is a hundred and eight walled wards, locked at the drums. Inside each, five households make a bao, and every one of them answers for the other four. At the lodging a ward chief is waiting with a lamp and a register. He does not look at the prince’s face. He counts heads the way a man counts sacks, and writes a number.
Ward chief: Silla embassy. Eleven mouths. / Eleven in, eleven out. If one of you dies, report it to the ward before the morning drum. / We’ll send a man to make up the count.
chunchu: Make up the count. / …With whom?
Ward chief: With a man.
chunchu: Any man?
Ward chief: The register hasn’t got a column for names, sir. Only for the number.
Inmun reads the register over the man’s shoulder. Eleven. He will live in this city for most of his life, and in every count it ever makes of him he will be one stroke in that column.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Jindeok, yr. 2 (648); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 128] Chunchu knelt and memorialized: my country lies in a corner of the sea, and Baekje, strong and cunning, has repeatedly invaded; if Your Majesty does not lend the heavenly troops to cut away this evil, the people of our humble city will all be taken captive. Taizong deeply agreed, and promised to send an army.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Jindeok, yr. 2 (648); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 128 · cf. Jiu Tangshu (舊唐書) bk. 199上, Account of Silla] When he arrived, seeing that Chunchu’s bearing was outstanding, they treated him generously.
taizong: Your name is “Spring and Autumn”…? Then is your younger brother called “Warring States”?
chunchu: My father revered the Confucian learning, and named me after Confucius’s “Spring and Autumn Annals”.
chunchu: Since the age of the Three Zhou, Samhan and the Central Plain have been inseparable. / And now Your Majesty has accomplished the great work of restoring the glory of Han — / are you not the Guangwu of this age?
chunchu: Silla will accept investiture from the Great Tang. / Your Majesty has armies beyond counting; Chunchu has knowledge of Samhan. / Samhan is known best by the people of Samhan. / To accomplish a great work, must not great men gather?
taizong: Yes — there is something between us that fits.
taizong: Your Divine Country sends me the most cunning man in Samhan. / Good. I have already spent a summer failing against the Eternal General. I prefer allies who can count.
After the hall, a smaller room. A go board. The emperor keeps the platform. Chunchu sits on the floor. Stones click in the dark.
taizong: Li Shimin.
chunchu: …Sir?
taizong: You asked my name, did you not. / That is my name. / Li Shimin.
The room does not react, because the room does not understand what has just happened. Only two men in it do.
No law forbids what he has just done; something older and more total than law forbids it. He has handed a foreign prince the one thing his own sons cannot say out loud.
chunchu: A magnificent name. / So an emperor is a man like the rest of us. / …Though it will be a dreadful nuisance to avoid writing it.
Chunchu makes the joke because he can feel that the man needs to be laughed with — now, this instant — or the moment will curdle into something neither of them can carry out of the room. People call the gift diplomacy. He knew, in a heartbeat, what the man in front of him was afraid would happen next.
taizong: Chunchu. It is a waste, a man like you growing old on the frontier. / Come and serve in my imperial guard. / A house in Chang’an, a title, and bring your son as well.
chunchu: …You honour me, Your Majesty.
taizong: “You honour me” means “no.”
chunchu: Your Majesty reads people well.
taizong: I read people well. It is why I am still alive. / That, and Saluzi.
chunchu: Saluzi, Majesty? / …Forgive me. I don’t know the name.
taizong: No, you would not. He never held office. / No title, no fief, no son at court for me to promote. Outside Luoyang he took an arrow in the chest that had my name on it, and brought me back to camp with it still in him. / The most loyal warrior I have ever had. Perhaps I shall introduce you, before you go.
chunchu: …I would very much like that, Majesty.
taizong: That one means “yes.” Good.
Chunchu files the name the way he files everything in this city. A man who took an arrow for the emperor and asked for nothing afterwards is either a saint or a lever, and either way worth an introduction.
taizong: Fine. Leave the son, then. Do not say “no” to that one.
Inmun stays in Chang’an. He will be there, on and off, for the rest of his life.
Between audiences Chunchu watches the machinery. A clerk bows. An order moves. A province three months away changes its taxes because one man in yellow silk nodded. No Harmony Council. No uncle with a veto. No night of unanimity.
He also asks, as idly as a foreign envoy can ask anything, after a general named Saluzi. A clerk of the Ministry of War spends an afternoon in the rolls on his behalf and comes back apologetic. There is no Saluzi: no rank, no fief, no tomb, no widow drawing a pension. Either the emperor’s most loyal warrior is dead, or he is the only man in Chang’an without paperwork. Chunchu finds he wants to meet him more than he wanted to meet the emperor.
