The Ministry of War can’t find him a general, so Chunchu tries the historians. Chu Suiliang receives him among the shelves. He once refused to let the emperor read his own diary. Now he’s high enough to choose what he says, and careful enough to say very little.
chunchu: Lord Chu. A small question from a small country. / His Majesty came to the throne by way of the Xuanwu Gate, I’m told. The ninth year of Wude, the sixth month, the fourth day—
chusuiliang: Which gate?
chunchu: …The Xuanwu Gate. The north one.
chusuiliang: There is a gate there. A very fine gate. Nothing happened at it.
chunchu: And the fourth day of the sixth month?
chusuiliang: The third was a fine day, Prince. The fifth was finer. / I can recommend either.
chunchu: I’d heard the account was rewritten.
chusuiliang: Harmonized, Prince. / Here we say harmonized.
chunchu: Then I’ll take the fifth. / I’ve always liked a fine day.
The rest he hears at the envoys’ lodging, where foreigners trade what the palace will not. The emperor got the record from his chancellor in the end, read the pages about the gate, and sent them back to be written more plainly. Nobody has forbidden the fourth day of the sixth month since. It has simply stopped coming round.
On the morning before he is to leave, a parcel comes to the lodging from the palace. Inside are rubbings of two steles in the emperor’s own hand, and a new history of the Jin dynasty, so fresh from the Historiography Office that the paste on the bindings is still soft.
inmun: The paste is still wet, Father. / Is this one… harmonized?
chunchu: Fresh. Here they harmonize it before the paste dries. / Read it slowly anyway. We’ll want to know what the Jin are allowed to have done.
He asks for one more thing before he goes: Tang court dress, cut to Silla measure, so that his officials at home will look like the officials in this city. The emperor is delighted, and sends a chest of it.
chunchu: Your Majesty… forgive a barbarian’s question. / You mean… they all absolutely obey you, no matter what?
taizong: If they do not, they stop being useful. / Useful men live longer. I did not invent that. I only wrote it down.
chunchu: And if the great families were to meet, Majesty. All of them, in one room. And agree that you should no longer be emperor? / …What happens then?
Taizong looks at him for a long moment, as though Chunchu had asked what happens if the sun is voted out of the sky. Then he laughs, and it is not a polite laugh.
taizong: Agree? Agree to what, precisely? / A man does not agree to stop being emperor. It happens to him at the end of a knife, and then there is a new emperor, and the families agree with him. / Meet in a room. Vote. / (laughs again) / Do you hear yourself, Spring-and-Autumn? Who would carry the result to me? Who would be fool enough to read it aloud?
chunchu: In Silla, Majesty, someone did. The Harmony Council deposed a king. He was my grandfather. / They met, they agreed, and he went home.
taizong: He went home. / They told a king he was no longer king, and he… went home. He did not kill them? Not even one, to make the point?
chunchu: …Not even one, Majesty.
Taizong shakes his head, still smiling, and goes back to his memorials. Chunchu says nothing more. He is watching the brush in the emperor’s hand: one man, one brush, and at the far end of it a province three months away. Nobody in this palace will ever meet in a room to vote that hand off the paper. He cannot stop looking at it, the way a poor man looks at a jade he will never afford, and he does not let one particle of it reach his face.
taizong: You Samhan people have the strangest notions of government. / You vote your kings off their thrones like stewards caught with the wine. You put a woman on the throne, and when she dies you put another one there, and then you come to me astonished that your neighbours take liberties. / And your uncles sit up all night until they agree, and call it harmony. / (smiles, fond and superior) / A throne is a blade with a seat attached, Spring-and-Autumn. Stop setting it for dinner.
Chunchu laughs because the insult is also a compliment, and because he has just seen the future of Samhan politics wearing an emperor’s face — chauvinist, competent, impossible to un-admire.
The days between audiences belong to someone else. The crown prince — Li Zhi, twenty years old and still allowed to laugh with his shoulders — steals Chunchu from the memorial-hall the way a younger brother steals an older one from a funeral, and takes him to the imperial gyuku ground.
gaozong: If my father keeps you in that hall any longer you will turn into a memorial stele. / Gyuku. I have Tang clubs that have never met a Silla swing. They are about to be humbled — or you are.
chunchu: Your Highness. If I fall and die, your father will declare war on my corpse.
gaozong: Then do not fall. / I am told you are good at not dying when it would be inconvenient.
They play gyuku until the dust makes them the same colour. Li Zhi’s club is palace-issue lacquer — beautiful, slightly wrong in the hands. Chunchu’s is travel-worn Wolseong pine he refused to replace for the embassy, which the Tang attendants find either humble or insane. Li Zhi talks like a man who has been waiting his whole life to be ordinary with somebody dangerous. Chunchu lets him — between strokes, between arguments about whose wood is “premium,” between the kind of silence that founds alliances.
gaozong: That club… you unpacked that from the embassy chests. / We have better in the palace. Southern bamboo. Steamed three times.
chunchu: Your Highness. A good club is not the forest… it is the ball you hit. / And I am not ready to divorce this shaft.
gaozong: …Fair. / Then one more round with your marriage.
gaozong: When I am emperor — / No. That sounds like a curse. When the years have been kinder — / I will still want this. A friend who does not need my title to stand upright.
chunchu: Then keep me as I am. / When you are emperor I will still be a man from a small country with a large grudge. / That is the only honest introduction I have.
gaozong: Good. / Brothers, then — of the inconvenient kind.
chunchu: Of the inconvenient kind.
Inmun watches from a covered walk and says nothing. He has learned already that some alliances are written in edicts, and some are written in dust on a horse’s flank.
## The Six Steeds
That night the emperor dismisses the lamp-bearers and carries the lamp himself, down a gallery behind the Liangyi Hall that no envoy has been shown. Along the wall runs a band of six stone horses, each long panel cut in low relief from drawings by the court painter. They are meant for the mountain at Zhaoling, where they will stand guard over a tomb. Nobody has told Chunchu whose.
The doors close behind them on a corridor so long the lamp cannot find the end of it. Taizong does not wait for ceremony. He takes the Silla prince by the elbow, the way one steers a friend through a crowded market, and walks him into the dark.
taizong: Leave the lamp to me tonight. I have carried heavier things down darker corridors. / You have seen my clerks, Spring-and-Autumn, and my six boards, and my very tedious seal. You have not yet met the ones who actually made me emperor. / Allow me to present them.
chunchu: …Horses, Your Majesty?
He lifts the lamp to the first panel. Out of the black comes a horse in mid-stride, cut so shallow it seems to be passing through the wall rather than standing on it. The emperor lays his palm on its hoof, as if to keep it from leaving.
taizong: Baitiwu. Black from ear to tail, and white at all four feet, as though he had walked through snow and declined to wipe them. / I was twenty. A warlord held the whole of the west, and we broke him at Qianshuiyuan before noon. My generals wished to rest. I did not. / Baitiwu ran all night. Two hundred li. He woke to find me at his gate, and simply… surrendered. I have never in my life been so exhausted, nor so pleased with anyone.
They walk on. The lamp swings at his side, and their two shadows climb the wall ahead of them, larger than either man, stepping over the carved hooves.
taizong: Telebiao. Yellow, with a pale muzzle. He came to us off the steppe with a Turkic name, and I hadn’t the heart to take it from him. / A northern warlord had seized Taiyuan. My father’s own city, Chunchu, the very city we marched out of. I ran him down through the Queshu valley: eight engagements in a single day, two days without food, three without my armour off. / Telebiao did not complain once. I complained without ceasing. He carried me regardless.
At the third panel he does not stop. The lamp slides over a horse with a man standing at its chest, and the emperor walks on as though he has not seen it.
taizong: Not that one. Not yet.
Ten paces on, the emperor stops so abruptly that Chunchu nearly walks into his sleeve. This time he holds the lamp high over his head, and a grey horse comes out of the stone at full gallop.
taizong: Qingzhui. Grey-dappled, and fast as a rumour. / At Hulao, a rival who called himself king came with a hundred thousand men to relieve Luoyang. I had perhaps three thousand five hundred riders, and I elected to be rude about the arithmetic. / Five arrows struck him, Chunchu. Every one of them from behind.
chunchu: From behind… all five?
taizong: All five. They could not hit him from the front. By the time they drew, he was already past them.
He does not wait for Chunchu to catch up. The next horse is already in the light.
taizong: Shifachi. Red as a seal. The name is a Turkic title, and he wore it like one. / He carried me against both of them in the same spring: the one shut up in Luoyang, and the one who came to save him. Five arrows in the hindquarters, and he finished the charge regardless, bristling like a hedgehog that had lost its temper. / Two pretenders taken in one season, on that horse. And still the historians insist on crediting me.
At the sixth panel he brings the lamp close enough to warm the stone, and counts along the horse’s flank with one finger, arrow by arrow, the way a man counts the graves of his own soldiers.
taizong: And Quanmaogua. Curly-coated, black-muzzled, quite the ugliest horse in the empire, and the most stubborn. / The last of the rebels, by the Ming River. Nine arrows: six in front, three behind. Count them, if you like; the masons were most particular. / He stood until the fighting was done. Then he lay down, as though he had only been waiting for permission.
They reach the end of the gallery. Past the sixth horse the timber frame runs on, and inside it the stone is smooth.
chunchu: And the seventh, Your Majesty? For Liaodong?
taizong: There is no seventh. I rode to Liaodong on a perfectly good horse whose name I find I have mislaid.
Then he turns and walks back the way they came, past the arrows, past the red horse and the grey, and Chunchu follows the lamp. He stops at the third panel, the one he would not look at, and this time he lifts the light all the way up.
taizong: Saluzi.
Chunchu hears the name before he understands it. He looks at the purple horse in the stone, and at the man carved at its chest, and back at the emperor, and an afternoon of the Ministry of War’s rolls rearranges itself in his head. Five horses, five names, and not once has it occurred to him.
chunchu: …Saluzi. / Your most loyal warrior. The one who never held office. / Majesty. He is a horse.
taizong: The finest in the empire. I never said he was a man, Spring-and-Autumn. You supplied that yourself. / Most of my ministers make the same mistake about themselves.
chunchu: I had a clerk of your Ministry of War search the rolls for him. / All afternoon.
taizong: (laughs, and it carries all the way down the gallery) / Did you. Then somewhere in my ministry there is a clerk who believes the Silla prince is hunting my generals. I shall have to promote him.
Then the laugh goes out of him the way a lamp gutters, and he looks back up at the stone.
taizong: Purple, the colour of a fresh bruise, and quite as proud of himself. / Outside Luoyang I galloped too far ahead, as young men will, and found myself entirely alone with the pretender’s army, which was deciding what to do with me. An arrow took Saluzi in the chest. He did not fall. He stood there with it in him and waited for me to think of something. / One of my generals rode in, gave me his own horse, and drew the arrow out of mine with his bare hands while the enemy looked on. That is he, at the chest. The only man I have permitted onto these walls. / Saluzi carried me back to camp, and then he died. He waited until it was convenient for me. I have never quite forgiven him the courtesy.
He does not move on. He sets the lamp on the floor beneath the panel, which is not a thing emperors do in front of foreign princes, and lays his hand flat on the carved neck, and leaves it there.
taizong: I have had sons, Spring-and-Autumn. Wives. More ministers than I can name. / He is the only one who never once asked me for anything.
Chunchu does not interrupt. It is the first time in Chang’an he has seen the emperor need an audience rather than command one.
taizong: These are going to the mountain. When I am laid in Zhaoling, the six of them will stand outside the door and wait. / He shall have the place nearest. He always did insist on being out in front.
chunchu: Then they’ll have a long wait, Majesty. And horses do so hate waiting.
Taizong picks up the lamp and turns. It hangs low at his knee now, and from below his face is all hollows.
taizong: I am not joking, you.
The Second Emperor reveals he is dying.
taizong: Chunchu. You grew up in Samhan, so—
taizong: Chunchu… promise me this one thing. / Accomplish this one great work for me…! / Goryeo is the single failure of my life. / Baekje will be the single failure of yours. / I—your country—
He sets the lamp down again at the foot of the purple horse.
taizong: I do not go to Liaodong for land. I have mountains and rivers enough to bore a man to death. / When the two of them are settled, everything south of Pyongyang, and the whole of Baekje, is Silla’s. For your peace. Forever.
chunchu: …May I have that in writing, Majesty?
taizong: (laughs) An emperor’s word is the writing, Spring-and-Autumn. / Every clerk in this city will remember it for you.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 7, Silla Annals — King Munmu, yr. 11 (671): Munmu’s reply to Xue Rengui, quoting the Second Emperor in the twenty-second year of Zhenguan (648)] I attack Goguryeo now for no other reason than pity for you, Silla, caught between two countries, invaded every year without a year’s peace. Mountains, rivers and land are not what I covet; jade, silk, sons and daughters I already have. When I have pacified the two countries, the land south of Pyongyang and the land of Baekje shall all be given to you, Silla, for your lasting peace.
At a banquet meant to impress the Silla guest, the Second Emperor’s laughter is the loudest thing in the hall. Behind a screen a concubine listens the way a strategist listens — counting who drinks, who flinches, which foreign prince the emperor calls brother.
west_ambassador: (Tang court, wine raised) / To the Khan of Heaven — who makes even Samhan learn the proper direction to bow.
east_ambassador: (Yamato envoy, smiling carefully) / And to the guest who weeps beautifully enough to move an empire. / We of the East know the value of a well-timed tear.
chunchu: Gentlemen. If tears were an army, Silla would have conquered you both already. / (the room laughs; he has bought himself a second of safety)
west_ambassador: (not laughing) / The prince’s jest hurts the feelings of ten million households of the Great Tang.
taizong: Listen to him. A barbarian who understands banquet combat. / Zhi — keep this one. Men who can joke while kneeling are rarer than honest generals.
Above the dais hangs one more banner, gold on red: LUXURY IS THE ENEMY. Under it a thousand dishes go round, each carried by a servant in the same livery, at the same pace, with the same face. When the emperor lifts his cup the whole hall shouts Ten thousand years! on one breath, and sits again on the next.
east_ambassador: (reading the banners along the wall, half to himself) / Eight directions under one roof… / We must borrow that one. We have rather a lot of islands, so we’ll want a bigger roof.
Behind the screen Wu does not merely listen. She works the room without entering it — a glance that steadies a nervous maid, a smile that makes the Western Ambassador drink slower, a silence that pulls the Eastern envoy’s eyes toward the foreign prince.
wuzetian: (soft, to Chunchu when the toast turns) / So it is true. Your country seats a woman as king. / How daring. How… instructive.
chunchu: Heaven chose her. We only stopped arguing long enough to notice.
wuzetian: (laughs — warm, precise, a little too close) / Heaven is so often credited after the clever have already moved the chairs. / Tell me — when she speaks, do the uncles still pretend the voice is a man’s?
west_ambassador: A woman king… picturesque. Like a story told to frighten boys.
east_ambassador: In our islands we have empresses. Power wears many sleeves. / (glances at Wu, then away — too slow)
wuzetian: (to Chunchu alone, smiling as if they share a private theater) / I like a man who brings dangerous news and still finds time to flirt with an empire. / Stay for one more cup. Or must Silla’s tears dry on schedule?
wuzetian: He likes the one who weeps well. / Noted.
[FLASHBACK -108 Gija & Wiman]
  This is the story of migration from the West into Samhan.
  Jizi, a sage of the West, escapes from the chaos of his homeland and is put in charge of the people of Joseon.
  He institutes the Eight Prohibitions, a draconian system of laws to rule over the people.
  Wiman, a general of Yan, in the West, seeks refuge in the court of King Jun. He eventually stages a coup, and King Jun flees south.
  The Eight Prohibitions are the oldest written law in this record and only three of them survive. Kill a man, die for it. Injure a man, pay in grain. Steal, and become the household property of the man you stole from — and if you buy your way out, nobody will marry you afterwards anyway.
  herald: That last clause is the frightening one.
  herald: The law does not kill you. / People do.
  Wiman arrives with a thousand men, his hair in the Joseon topknot and Joseon clothes on his back, which is either respect or the most patient disguise in this history.
  herald: The king has given him the western border, they say.
  herald: The border. To a refugee.
  herald: He’s a refugee — where else would he go? He’ll be loyal.
  He sends word that the enemy is coming and he must bring his men in to protect the king. He brings his men in. There is no enemy.
  King Jun goes south by sea with what is left of his household and calls himself the King of Han, and the people who go with him become the ancestors of the three Han. The three Han take their name from that.
## HALLWAY
Night in a long palace corridor. Red columns, white plaster, a little light leaking from the next hall. Somewhere a banquet is still going. Out here it’s quiet enough to hear footsteps behind you.
Before the embassy horses leave Chang’an, a woman from the emperor’s household asks for a moment that is not on any schedule. The clerks pretend not to see. That is how courts invent privacy.
wuzetian: Chunchu!
chunchu: ?
He turns in the dark.
wuzetian: Chunchu… you are the one from the country with the woman king, correct?
chunchu: Yes, ma’am.
wuzetian: How is she doing?
chunchu: Well, the conservative faction initially had its doubts about whether a woman could take the throne. / However, as with all things in life, the problem turned out to be more in the mind than in reality. / She has proven to be a wise and capable king, and is well-beloved by the p—
wuzetian: Yes, yes. But that wasn’t my question… / How is she doing?
chunchu: …Oh. / (smiling) She is doing well. She has found a lot of peace in her life. Thank you for asking.
wuzetian: Can you deliver her a message for me? / Tell her to never stand down in the face of hardship. / In the violent and competitive world of men, tell her I want her to become a defiant woman — a woman who can look any man in the face and see an equal. A woman who can conquer worlds with her glance. / Tell her to stay silent — not in submission, but in strength. / For if there is anything I have learned in the Emperor’s Court, it is that silence is the true mark of power…! / (determined, fierce)
chunchu: (astonished) …Oh, I see. / W-who did you say you were again?
wuzetian: (leans over to his ear, whispers something)
Whatever she says takes less than a breath. When she draws back she is still smiling — the social smile of a woman who could host a banquet or end a lineage with the same mouth.
chunchu: (paralyzed in fear, wide-eyed, scurries away back toward Silla)
wuzetian: (waves back flirtatiously)
gaozong: (calling from behind) Wu! You haven’t been scaring our guests away, have you?
## The Mingde Gate
On the last morning Li Zhi rides down to the Mingde Gate himself, which crown princes do not do.
At the gate Chunchu does not bow like a foreign guest. He bows like a man watching his younger brother try on a coat that will never come off.
gaozong: Spring and Autumn. / You really are going.
chunchu: I said I would. / Inconvenient brothers keep their appointments.
gaozong: Then when you are king — / write to me as you wrote when we were only dust and horses. / I will need one person who remembers my name was Zhi before it was an era.
chunchu: Yes…! / Now—— we have won this war…!
Chunchu says it the way a man says a prayer he has been saving.
He leaves Chang’an with the alliance sealed and his son still inside the wall. The gates do not ask who was afraid.
I’ve met many powerful people in my life. Generals, kings, emperors. But there has only been one person who I’ve been afraid of. During that short conversation, that woman’s eyes paralyzed me in fear.
## On Gunhae
A day and a night out to sea, a second hull takes their wind. Not a war fleet. A Goguryeo patrol boat, the kind that sniffs a sea-road and reports who used it. They’ve been sniffing this one since Chunchu walked out of Yeon’s prison.
ongunhae: My lord. The small boat.
chunchu: That cap is heavy.
ongunhae: Then I will wear it.
On Gunhae takes the high cap and the great coat — Tang’s gift, cut to be read at two li as a prince. He sits high on the deck, where the mast makes a chair of shadow, and does not wave.
The patrol closes. A shout across the water names the wrong man, and is satisfied. They board. They take the coat. The annal will say they killed him. Chunchu’s small boat is already a darker strip of sea.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Jindeok, yr. 2 (648); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 128] On the way home, at sea, Chunchu met Goguryeo patrol soldiers. His attendant On Gunhae sat on the ship in a high cap and a great coat; the patrol took him for Chunchu and seized and killed him. Chunchu reached the country in a small boat. The queen heard, grieved, posthumously made Gunhae a Daeachan, and richly rewarded his descendants.
He reaches the home shore in a boat Chang’an wouldn’t have bothered to count.
Chunchu has watched one brush move an empire. Now he wants that brush in Silla. The Harmony Council hasn't noticed yet…!

=== EPISODE 49: Royal Secretariat (651)
For three months a border petition has been circling the Harmony Council like a bird that cannot find a roof. Chunchu has counted the seals. He has counted the men who must touch a paper before a soldier may move. He has stopped counting aloud, because the room mistakes counting for patience.
[diagram royal-secretariat]
[diagram harmony-council]
He clears a side hall in the palace — small enough that the old clans will call it irregular, large enough for the work. Three clerks. One courier captain. A table that has never held a feast. He practices the sentence the way other men practice a sword form.
What he brought home from the west is a grammar. One seal. One speed. Fewer uncles. When the old council finally falls, nobody will proclaim it. It will just be a table that has never held a feast.
chunchu: A petition.
chunchu: A seal.
chunchu: A courier.
chunchu: Are you getting it?
chunchu: These are not three separate offices.
chunchu: This is one office.
chunchu: We call it the Royal Secretariat.
chunchu: Today, the king will reinvent the kingdom.
Nobody laughs. The youngest clerk writes the name down as if the words had always been waiting for ink. Outside, the Harmony Council is still debating the same petition. Inside, the petition has somewhere to land.
Chunchu establishes the Royal Secretariat — an institution that reports to the king alone. The clans will call it a shortcut. He will call it Tuesday.
jukji: Petition. Seal. Courier. / I can do that before the Council finishes clearing its throat.
chunchu: Then you are 중시 — Premier of the Royal Secretariat. / True Bone. Young Hwarang. My confidante. / In Chang’an the emperor does not wait for every uncle to agree. I watched that power and wanted it for this country — not for my vanity. For speed.
The Harmony Council still meets on the appointed days, in polished chairs, reciting the unanimity rule to a room that no decision of consequence waits for anymore. They have been made lame ducks without the dignity of abolition — and they know it by the third week, when a border petition returns sealed before their debate has chosen a speaker.
In the market a storyteller invents a joke that sticks: Our prince is in love with the emperor. Another version: enamored with China. Chunchu hears both and does not correct them. Munhee, packing a different set of bags, corrects them for him.
munhee: He is in love with a door that opens when he knocks. / Call that China if you like. I call it not waiting for twelve men to finish a sentence.
jukji: The Council asked what my title means. / I told them: 侍中 — I stand beside the work. / They did not laugh. That was how I knew it had worked.
## Tang Dress
The chest of court robes from the west is opened at the new year. By spring every senior official has been measured for one. A year later the kingdom stops counting its own years and starts counting the emperor’s. Bupmin sails west with the queen’s ode woven into a length of silk. The emperor in Chang’an admires it extravagantly.
munmu: Father. The collar itches.
chunchu: Everything new itches. / Wear it to the Council, and watch which uncles scratch.
## Tsukushi
In the summer of 651 a Silla tribute ship puts in at Tsukushi with its envoys dressed in the new robes. The Yamato court takes one look at them and sends them home.
Kose no Ōmi: If we do not strike Silla now, we will regret it later. / Fill the sea from Naniwa to Tsukushi with ships, bow to stern, and call them to account. It would be easy.
Emperor Kōtoku does not fill the sea. His successors will remember the idea.
Rewind to Chang'an. The room is too warm, the crown prince hasn't moved since dawn, and someone in the anteroom is taking notes…!

=== EPISODE 50: Jiabeng (駕崩) (649)
## The Cuiwei Palace
The emperor dies in the Cuiwei Palace in the fifth month. He is fifty-one. The room is kept too warm, and the silk on the bed is the colour of late wheat.
The crown prince has been sitting since before dawn. He is twenty-one. He has the shoulders for the armour and not yet the face for the title. When the breathing stops, he does not move for a long time — long enough that the ministers begin to look at one another instead of at the bed.
gaozong: ……Father. / Not yet——
Someone touches his elbow. Someone else is already writing. The empire does not wait for grief to finish its sentence.
The court kneels, and the young man rises — the same hands that would not leave the bed now accepting the seal, the edict, the yellow silk that means the West has a new centre.
gaozong: I receive the late emperor’s last command. / From this day—— / ……We will listen.
He does not say I. He says the word that empties a man of his own name. The hall answers like a single throat.
The will is long on mourning and short on everything else, except one line, which the new emperor reads twice. The war in Liaodong is to stop.
The great emperor is given a temple name — Taizong. The clerks write it in the register and close the book.
gaozong: The great emperor’s temple name is hereby set as Taizong (太宗).
The empire is told how to grieve. The edict fixes the days of mourning by rank, and at dusk in every ward of Chang’an the ward chief walks the lanes and listens at the doors, to be sure the weeping inside is of the proper length.
Two of his dragons, the Red and the White, both of them Turks, petition to be killed and laid beside him, to guard the tomb the way the six stone horses will. It is the highest loyalty the steppe knows. The court is moved. The young emperor reads the petition twice.
gaozong: Denied. / …Father already has six horses waiting at his door. / He would scold Us for wasting two good generals.
In Chang’an the new emperor is still learning how to stand. In Sabi, another king is learning how to be afraid.
King Euija grows more watchful of the Great Clans. Tang has gone quiet, and quiet from that direction rarely stays put.
Gyebek already knows what the silence means. A house that fights itself does not need an emperor to finish it.
The news crosses the sea in the eighth month. In Surabol, Chunchu reads the will through to the line about Liaodong, and then reads that line again.
chunchu: He made me promise to finish it. / And then he left orders to stop. / …Very well. Then it is mine.
In an anteroom a young concubine waits with the other women who must not be seen grieving too loudly. Her name is not yet heavy. Her attention already is. She watches how a seal moves from a dead hand to a living one — and files the lesson where ambition keeps its dry goods.
wuzetian: (soft, to no one) / So that is how an empire changes owners. / Quietly. With someone else speaking the first sentence.
The late emperor’s women who bore him no children are sent to the Ganye Temple, to shave their heads and pray for him for the rest of their lives. Wu goes with them.
A year later, on the anniversary, the new emperor comes to the temple to burn incense for his father. A nun in grey looks up at him from the second row, and does not look down again.
gaozong: Lady Wu. / …They cut your hair.
wuzetian: Hair grows back, Majesty. / (and already the room tilts a degree toward her)
Seven years of a polite queen and a busy nephew. Sooner or later, Silla has to admit who's really sitting in the chair…!

=== EPISODE 51: King Muyeol (654)
For seven years the crown has sat on Queen Jinduk. The work has sat on her nephew’s table. Nobody has ever called her foolish. She’s simply outnumbered by seals.
jinduk: Nephew. / When I die, do not pretend I ruled. / Say I kept the chair warm until the country was ready to admit who was already sitting in it.
chunchu: Aunt. / You ruled the only way left to Sacred Bone — by lasting.
Kangrim reads her name three times — Jinduk. Jinduk. Jinduk. — the ledger's habit before a Sacred Bone line closes.
kangrim: Majesty. / Sacred Bone ends on your breath. One question. / Did you keep the crown warm for the next hand — or keep it from cooling into a man’s?
jinduk: …I kept a seat from becoming a joke. / That is all the Sacred Bone had left to do.
kangrim: Then the minutes are clean. / Walk.
Queen Jinduk is dead. With her, the Sacred Bone bloodline has finally gone extinct.
The Harmony Council meets again to enthrone the next king.
Again the rule is unanimity. Again the room discovers how long a single withheld hand can last — until Alchun laughs the holdout down, and the first True Bone king Silla has ever crowned is made by the same math that once made a queen.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — King Muyeol, accession (654); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 134] Your servant is old, and has no virtuous conduct worth naming. In virtue and standing none now is weightier than Lord Chunchu; he may truly be called a hero who can save the age.
alchun: Come now~ is there anyone who doesn’t know it will be Chunchu~~
alchun: A True Bone on the throne. First since there was a throne. / …Somebody had probably better write that down.
alchun: This servant can find no reason to object. / Nor could anyone else.
alchun: The age of Kim Chunchu begins.
Munhee becomes queen. Years ago her sister sold her a dream on a hill. She married in disgrace, to a man with no claim to anything. Now she stands beside his throne.
munhee: My sister sold me that dream for one silk skirt. / In hindsight she undercharged.
yushin: Your Majesty… even so…. / To lead the country down a road of ruin for a private grudge — that is not the act of a wise king…!
chunchu: ….What? A private grudge? / Is that truly how you have all seen me? / An old man maddened by his daughter’s death, sharpening revenge? / How… disappointing. / I am a man looking at the thousand-year flourishing of the sacred country. / I was raised on the study of kingship from childhood…
yushin: I do not know whether to fear him or admire him…. / And yet— / Kim Chunchu…
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 5, Silla Annals — Queen Jindeok, death notice (654); Lee Byong-do ed., vol. 1, p. 134] The people of the country said: from the founder Hyeokgeose to Jindeok, twenty-eight sovereigns, they called Sacred Bone; from Muyeol to the last kings, they called True Bone.
That night a letter leaves Surabol for Chang’an, written in a hand that still remembers the Wei River. It begins without titles: Zhi — I kept the appointment. Do not let the coat eat you.
I wrote to Zhi as a brother. I did not write what I had seen in that woman’s eyes. Some warnings cannot be put in a letter without becoming a prophecy you cannot take back.
gaozong: He became king. / Of course he did. / Send him horses. And tell him the dust here still has room for one more inconvenient man.
Far west, the Third Emperor’s court learns a new gravity. The young woman who once waited in an anteroom now finishes sentences the emperor starts. Clerks say her influence is growing by the day. They say it softly.
Before Bupmin was anybody's heir, he was a prince with bad arithmetic. Ten years back, a harbour girl is about to tell him so…!

=== EPISODE 52: Jahee (644)
Yushin sends Bupmin to the coast to work under Kim Seonpum. It is a season with a tide book instead of a training yard. The quay does not care that he is a prince. It cares whether the sums close.
Her name is Jahee. Tonight she is the daughter who keeps Seonpum’s inkstones, and she has already decided his arithmetic is sloppy.
jayi: Your sums are wrong. / The tide does not care that you are a prince. / Count again. / While I am watching.
munmu: …Where. / No — / Please show me.
She corrects the sum with a brush he was not supposed to steal. Warehouse lamp. Salt on the page. He watches her mouth instead of the numbers, and she lets him, once, because the tide will not wait for dignity.
Rain finds the eave. They stand inside a hard rain-curtain with a wet ledger between them, and almost do the stupid thing, and do not — until there is a stolen brush between their mouths, and then they do.
jayi: Father is coughing. / From the warehouse shadow. / …Which is why it has to be now. / Before the tide comes in.
munmu: Do not close the book. / If you close it I… / will not know where to go.
Seonpum coughs once from the dark and pretends he did not see a prince learning the harbour by kissing the girl who can count. Years later the court will name her Jayi. The quay already had the true name.
## The Next King
Two queens come and go. Bupmin rides with the Hwarang through both. He never becomes the best gyuku player in Surabol. He becomes the one who remembers why the game was invented. When “a king for all” finally fits a grown mouth, the words already have dust on them.
munmu: Marshal. / When I said king for all — did I mean every kingdom, or every person who bleeds for one?
yushin: Ask the yard again tomorrow. / If the answer is only a speech, you are still six. / If it costs you a bruise — you are becoming Hwarang.
Bupmin wants to be a king for all. So did Silla’s first. To meet him, go back to a white horse kneeling…!

=== EPISODE 53: Hyukgose (-57) [flashback]
After the fall of Old Joseon, the local chiefs gather to select a new king when a White Horse suddenly leaves an egg — blue sky above, and later the court will keep the moon as its quiet sign.
At a well in the hills, the horse knelt and cried. Six chiefs dug where it stood. They lifted out a great egg. The shell opened on a boy who already looked like a king. He learns fast. The chiefs say the land has been waiting.
A young boy is born from the egg, whom the chiefs name Hyukgosé — to rule with brightness — and crown as king while he is still a boy; tradition says thirteen.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonder 1 — Founding of Silla (Hyeokgeose); Ha & Mintz tr., pp. 49–50] A white horse knelt and cried aloud; they dug the ground and found a great blue egg. They opened it, and there was a boy-child; they named him Hyeokgeose.
The chroniclers disagree about the colour of the egg and agree about the horse. Before anyone dug, the six chiefs saw it from the ridge of Mount Yang: a light hanging down beside Najeong like lightning that had forgotten to leave, and under it a white horse folded onto its knees, as if someone important were waiting in the grass.
alpyung: That’s… a horse, right? / Why’s a horse kneeling? Who to?
sobuldori: You ever seen a horse with wings? I haven’t. / …That one’s got wings, though.
alpyung: Slow. Go slow. If it spooks—
It does not spook. It lets them come close enough to see that its wings are folded the way a bird folds them and that its eyes are on the grass, not on them. Then it looks up and sees six grown men creeping at it through the pines with their sleeves held out like nets.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonders 1 — Silla Founder Hyeokgeose (新羅始祖 赫居世王)] Below Mount Yang, beside Najeong well, a strange vapour like a flash of lightning hung down to the ground, and there was a white horse kneeling as if in obeisance. They went to look and found a purple egg (one account says a great blue egg). The horse saw the men, gave a long neigh, and rose up to heaven.
Six chiefs stand in a wet field with their arms still out, holding nothing. Much later, when the country has a name and a calendar and a clerk for everything, the horse will be painted on a saddle-flap and buried with a king and called Chunma, the heavenly horse. That morning nobody calls it anything. Alpyung is the first to look down at what it was kneeling over.
alpyung: …It left something. / Dig. What are you all doing? Dig.
A few years later, Lady Alyoung is born from a Chicken Dragon’s rib at Alyeongjeong well — matched omen to matched omen — and she and Hyukgosé fall in love as two children the country already knew were throne-sized. They marry because they want each other. The omens agree.
herald: One from an egg, one from a chicken.
herald: …Did this country start in a kitchen?
Why did Old Joseon fall?
We’re going to create a brand new country — where families care for one another as one great house, and no one is left outside the gate.
The Royals will watch over all the people, like their very own children.
The Nobles will be wise and righteous, making decisions for the good of the nation.
We will divide the common people into 6 ranks, according to their virtues. This is going to be the start of a New Unity… Silla!
Six families end up running everything. In every new country, six families always do.
They say the first king learned love before law: one person to cherish, one person to serve — and the moon over Seorabeol was enough light for both.
hyukgose: I have heard that a true man needs only / one person to cherish, / and one person to serve, / and that is enough.
Sixty-one years later, the chronicle says, the king went up into the sky, and seven days after that his body came down again in five pieces, scattered over the ground. Nobody records a horse. Everybody in Seorabeol says there was one.
[QUOTE Samguk Yusa (三國遺事) bk. 1, Wonders 1 — Silla Founder Hyeokgeose (新羅始祖 赫居世王)] He ruled the country sixty-one years, and the king rose up to heaven. Seven days later his remains fell scattered to the ground… The people wished to bury them together, but a great serpent chased them off; so they buried the five parts separately and made the Five Tombs, also called the Serpent Tombs.
A chest rides the tide in, a magpie screaming over it. Whatever is inside needs a house. Preferably someone else’s…!

=== EPISODE 54: Talhae (-19) [flashback]
Late in the first king’s reign, a chest comes in on the tide at a fishing beach. A magpie flies over it, crying.
It has come a long way. A thousand li north-east of Wa, the queen of a country called Dapana carried a child for seven years and was delivered of an egg. The king said a person who lays an egg is an ill omen and should get rid of it. She could not. She wrapped it in silk, packed it in a chest with treasure, and gave it to the sea.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] Talhae was born in the land of Dapana, which lies a thousand li north-east of Wa. Its king had taken to wife the daughter of the king of the Land of Women. She was with child seven years, and then bore a great egg. The king said: “For a person to bear an egg is unlucky; it should be cast away.” She could not bear to, and wrapped the egg in silk, laid it in a chest with treasures, and set it afloat on the sea to go where it would.
It reaches Gaya first. The people of Golden Gaya see a strange chest bobbing off their beach and, being sensible, leave it there.
Gaya tells it differently, and with more nerve. In the Gaya chronicle Talhae comes ashore a grown man, walks into King Suro’s hall, and asks for the throne.
talhae: I’ve come for your throne. / You can fight me for it, or you can save us both the afternoon.
suro: …Heaven gave it to me. / I— it isn’t mine to give. Or to… lose.
So they fight the way kings fight in that country. Talhae becomes a hawk, and Suro becomes an eagle. Talhae becomes a sparrow, and Suro becomes a falcon. When Talhae is a man again he is standing in the middle of the hall with feathers on his shoulders, and he bows.
talhae: …That was a falcon. / Fine. I’ll find a country with a smaller king.
Either way, the chest goes on. At Ajinpo an old woman on the shore hauls it in with a rope and opens it, and there is a little boy inside, sitting among the treasure as if it were his luggage.
👵: Well. / You’re not a fish.
talhae: No. / Is this the country?
She names him herself, since there is nobody else to ask. A magpie followed the chest in, so she takes the bird out of the character for magpie, and what is left, Seok, is his surname. He got loose from the chest and came out of it, so he is Talhae, the one who got loose.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] Someone said: “Nobody knows this child’s surname. When the chest first came, a magpie flew after it, crying. Take part of the character for magpie and make Seok his surname. And since he undid the chest and came out of it, name him Talhae.”
He grows nine cheok tall, fishes to feed the old woman and never once complains about it, and when she tells him that a boy with bones like his should study, he studies geography. Mostly the part about where the good ground is.
## The Crescent House
Looking over the city, he picks the best ground in it, a crescent-shaped rise above the river, and finds that someone already lives there. The house belongs to Hogong, a minister who came over the sea from Wa long ago with a gourd tied at his waist to float on, and has the name to prove it.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Hyeokgeose, yr. 38] As for Hogong, his clan and surname are not known. He was a man of Wa, and at first he crossed the sea with a gourd tied at his waist; hence he was called Hogong, Lord Gourd.
Talhae does not have a house. He has a plan. One night he buries a whetstone and a sack of charcoal beside Hogong’s gate, and in the morning he goes to the magistrate and says the house was his family’s, taken while they were away.
hogong: I have lived in that house thirty years!
talhae: And my family lived there before you. We were smiths. / Dig by the gate, if you don’t believe me.
They dig. The whetstone and the charcoal come up out of the ground, black and convincing, and the magistrate gives Talhae the house.
hogong: …You buried those last night.
talhae: Prove it.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] He looked at Hogong’s house below Mount Yang and judged it auspicious ground; he laid a cunning plan, took it, and lived there. That ground later became Wolseong.
The ground becomes Wolseong, the Crescent Moon Fortress, where every king of Silla after him will live, which means every king of Silla lives in a stolen house. Nobody in the palace likes it when you mention this.
King Namhae hears about the clever young man in the crescent house and marries him to his daughter. Two kings later Talhae is sixty-two and on the throne himself, and one of the first things he does is make Hogong his chief minister, which is either an apology or the best joke in the annals.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] Second year, spring, first month: he appointed Hogong Grand Minister.
hogong: …Grand Minister.
talhae: You know the best ground in the city. I could use a man like that.
hogong: I knew it. You did bury them.
talhae: Prove it.
“Hogong. There’s a rooster in the woods.” It is the middle of the night. Roosters don’t crow at night…!

=== EPISODE 55: Alji (65) [flashback]
In the ninth year of his reign King Talhae wakes in the night to a rooster crowing in the woods west of the city, which roosters do not do at night.
talhae: Hogong. There’s a rooster in Sirim. / Go and see what it wants.
hogong: Majesty, it’s a rooster. It wants— / …Yes, Majesty. Going.
At first light Hogong walks into Sirim with a lantern he no longer needs, and finds a small box of gold hanging from a branch, and a white rooster underneath it, crowing at nothing.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] Ninth year, spring, third month: in the night the king heard a cock crowing among the trees of Sirim, west of Geumseong. At daybreak he sent Hogong to look, and there was a small gold-coloured chest hanging from a branch, and a white cock crowing beneath it.
They bring the box to the king and open it, and inside is a little boy, handsome and wide awake, who looks at the king as if the king were the one who had turned up in a box.
talhae: Well. / I came in a box too, you know. Mine was bigger.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] Hogong came back and reported it. The king had the chest brought and opened, and inside was a little boy of remarkable looks. The king was glad and said to those around him: “Is this not Heaven sending me a fine heir?” And he took him in and raised him.
Because he came out of a golden box, he is given the surname Kim, gold. Because he is a child, he is called Alji. The wood where the rooster crowed is renamed Gyerim, Rooster Wood, and for a while the whole country goes by that name.
[QUOTE Samguk Sagi (三國史記) bk. 1, Silla Annals — Talhae Isageum] When he grew up he was bright and full of wise plans, and he was named Alji. Since he had come out of a golden chest, his surname was Kim. Sirim was renamed Gyerim, and that became the name of the country.
Talhae has sons of his own and does not give Alji the throne, and Alji, by every account, does not ask for it. It takes his line seven generations to reach the crown. When they do, they keep it for six hundred years, call themselves the Kims of Surabol, and look down on a family from Gaya who have the same name for a different reason.
Under a certain hill beyond the city, the steam says the same word every time it leaves the water. It will be a long time before anybody answers it.
Back to Baekje. The king can’t sign a thing for three years. And the clans have a list with one name on it…!
